label: Umāmaheśvara Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ
description: The Umāmaheśvara temple is located in Cāka Bāhāḥ Ṭola and stands on a three-tier plinth. It has a composite roof type which combines a tiered roof and a dome. Before 1934 earthquake, the temple had three tiers and was constructed in the style of a pagoda. However, it was levelled by the earthquake and reconstructed in this mixed style. This temple is located approximately 8 m east of the Nārāyaṇa Temple ( LAL2740 ), and together they form a complex with streets passing by to the west and south. Residential houses surround the square, which has now almost turned into a market place; street vendors occupy most of the open space. The sanctum of the temple can be accessed via stone steps to the west. Two stone lions sit on the first plinth level to guard the deities inside. At the southwest corner of the plinth, one can find a hanging bell that was donated in 2012. A statue of Nandī (vehicle of Śiva) is in front of the temple, and a trident has been erected close to this icon. The entrance to the sanctum is clad in metal, and has a toraṇa with an image of Garuḍa on top and Umā-Maheśvara at the centre, flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra. The roofs as well as the columns are clad in copper. On top of the roof, one can see a pinnacle alongside a metal trident. A serpent covers the top of the pinnacle, while four other snakes creep up to the tip of the second roof from each of the bottom four corners. The main sanctum is a square room with doorways on all four sides. Inside, one can find a four-faced śivaliṅga clad in brass. Of the four doors, the western door is the main entry way. Surmounted by a torana , the entryway is encased in carved metal sheets and has a raised stone threshold (29 cm), while the other doors are much more simple and plain. A stone statue of Umāmaheśvara is attached to the eastern wall, and the sanctum also contains images of Śrīdevī, Bhūdevī, Viṣṇu and Sūrya (sitting on a chariot pulled by seven horses). The image of Sūrya (the Sun god) is a recreation of the archaic one, which was stolen some decades ago. Pruscha (1975 , 209) mentions that there was once an image of Candramā (the Moon god) here, though there is no other proof of this. The stone inscription attached above the southern door of the temple mentions that the monument was reconstructed by Viśvambhara Bhāro in NS 796 (CE 1676) during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla. The inscription further informs readers that the King and his son Yoganarendra Malla were also present at the consecration of the temple, where lands were bestowed and a guṭhī was established to fund its ritual worship However, these days no guṭhī lands connected to the temple could be traced. In VS 2058, local people collected donations in order to try to continue the daily and other ritual worships of the temple. They assigned a Brahmin from Agniśālā Ṭola to carry out this task. However, the earthquake 2015 further hindered the daily worship. The Cakravarti Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti (an organisation for local development) is currently responsible for opening and closing the temple.

label: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (1962 CE)
description: The caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala which are alligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the caitya is paved with black flagstone and has been encroached upon by building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira. Generally, caityas follow a pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, this caitya has Vairocana facing east, Mañjuśrī north, Vajrasattva west and Amitābha south. The caitya was built in 1962. A special worship was organised in the courtyard for the welfare of the community three months before its construction began. During the worship, donations were collected to fund its construction. On the full moon day of Āśvina an umbrella is placed on top of the caitya and on the full moon day of Vaiśākhaits the anniversary worship is performed.

label: Iku Bāhāḥ
description: Iku Bāhāḥ, a very small, private bāhāḥ, is located in Ikhālakhu Ṭola, about 35m northeast of the Ikhālakhu square. Since there is no entrance through any of the streets, one must enter through the door of a private building situated towards the west of the monument. At the centre of the courtyard, there is a small shrine facing east with just a small opening that is 55cm wide and raised on a one meter-high platform. Inside the shrine is a tiny image of Akṣobhya Buddha. One might notice the unusual proportions of the statue of the Buddha and the large lotus on which he is sitting. A small caitya, made from stone and with images of Tathāgatas facing in all four cardinal directions, forms the pinnacle of the shrine. In front of the shrine, there is a dharmadhātu caitya in octagonal shape. There are images of eight Lokeśvaras on the dharmadhātu : Vajrapāṇi, Gaganagañja, Ratnapāṇi, Kṣitigarbha, Padmapāṇi, Viśvapāṇi, Ratnagarbha and Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin. On the northern wall of the residential building, one can find a niche containing an aniconic stone statue that is worshiped as Gaṇeśa. At the west wall of the āgãchẽ is a khaḍga . The āgãchẽ of the Bāhāḥ is to the northernmost end of the courtyard, and it is possible to exit via the northeastern corner. Pruscha writes, “all that has remained of this Bahal is a small courtyard with plastered shrine and dharmadhatu in the form of a double petalled lotus. The shrine contains an image of Bhumisparsa Shakyamuni. It was constructed by Bekharatna Silakar in 1934 and its chief priest is a Bajracharya.” ( Pruscha 2015: 207) The illustration identified as Ikhālākhu Bāhāḥ on p. 141 in Locke 1985 is actually Iku Bāhāḥ, and the photograph of Ikhālākhu (mislabeled as Iku Bāhāḥ) is in fact on p. 139.

label: Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (1964 CE)
description: This Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and is part of a group of four caityas, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira. The Maṇḍala was constructed in 1964. The inscription does not mention the name of its founder, though locals state that his name was Harṣamuni Śākya.

label: Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ (1909 CE)
description: Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). It can be accessed via the entrance of a private building that is located at the southwest corner of the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ ( LAL2350 ). Bhīmarāja Śākya, a member of the saṅgha of Oku Bāhāḥ, established this bāhāḥ . The structure of the Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ differs from other bāhāḥ of Patan. This bāhāḥ has no no esoteric god house, and its courtyard (5.2 m x 5.2 m) contans an uncommon caitya. Located at the very center of the courtyard, this caitya is the main monument of the bāhāḥ and has a structure that is not often seen in the Valley. Four stone pillars have been erected at each of the four corners above its double-layered lotus petals (which together are 96cm in diameter), supporting a layer of stone that forms a roof. A statue of Avalokiteśvara stands on top of the lotus petals, and a stūpa -shaped finial has been placed on the roof . Śākya (1994, 35) calls it a Kūṭāgārākṛti Caitya. It is based on a square plinth measuring 185cm in width and 13cm in height. The sanctum has iron railings fixed on three sides, with the western face left free. A small, west-facing marble image of Avalokiteśvara stands inside the sanctum. Adorned in a crown, a large necklace, and a dhoti, the deity is performing varada with his right hand and holding the stem of a lotus in his left. The courtyard is paved in telia tiles and a plinth surrounds the residential buildings. The three-storey building on the northern side has a colonnaded three-bay phalcā underneath it. No inscription or any other document could be found to confirm the consecration date of this bāhāḥ . However, Bhīmarāja, the elder brother of Bhājudhana, established the bāhāḥ just after his younger brother established the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ in 1909 ( Śākya 1994, 120). Nowadays, some small cracks can be seen in the caitya. These were caused by the 2015 earthquake. Some aniconic stones images worshipped as Lukumāhādyaḥ have been placed at the northeastern corner of the courtyard. Śākya (1994, 121) mentions that a school named Mahābauddha Pāṭhaśālā once operated in this vihāra, and had 150 students. He also writes that there were wall paintings of Vīṇārāja, Khaḍgarāja, Dhvajarāja and Caityarāja on the wall of a house located to the south of the courtyard.

label: Devajyoti Bāhāḥ (1889 CE)
description: Devajyoti Bāhāḥ is a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ ( LAL0440 ). It is located to the north of Bu Bāhāḥ and can be accessed via a narrow alley that leads from the monument's north-west corner. The main shrine building faces north and stands on a double plinth. It is attached to the rear boundary wall, which is decorated with a pair of pilaster columns on either side. The monument appears to have been constructed relatively recently and has an overhanging concrete roof with a bell-shaped pinnacle and a st ūpa above it. The shrine is plastered in lime and has been painted white. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum. Small statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been attached to the boundary wall, on the left and right-hand sides of the shrine respectively. The courtyard (6.7 m x 4.2 m) is also home to a dharmadh ātu jin ālaya caitya (180 cm high) and a dharmadh ātu ma ṇḍala (90 cm high), both of which stand in front of the main monument and are lined up in its axis. The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings and has a colonnaded structure on the ground floor. Two bells hang from the stone pillars on the eastern and western sides of the courtyard. This bāhāḥ was established by Devajyoti Vajrācārya in 1889. After his death, his wives established a guṭhī for the management of the bāhāḥ in 1897. The Mūladuvā clan (a priest clan) of Bu Bāhāḥ performs the daily worship in this shrine. Aside from this, all other social and religious activities related to this bāhāḥ have come to an end.

label: Capĩgāḥ
description: Local residents still remember the open water channel [ deydha ḥ ( desadhala)] that used to run through Sunāguthi. A small pit ( kuṇḍa ) called Capĩgāḥ is located on the bank of this water channel and was once used to collect water. This water was considered to be holy and was offered to the statue of Bālakūmāri located in the temple to the east ( SUN0230 ). A local religious song also mentions bathing in the Capĩgāḥ. The royal water channel ( rājakulo ) dates back to the 9th century and used to supply water from Lele to Patan and the villages along its route. A road widening project undertaken in 2012 necessisted the closing of the formerly open water channel and the water was diverted into underground cement pipes. The Capĩgāḥ was filled with rubble, and the current water tank made of brick and cement was constructed in its place. This tank remains empty and appears to be neglected. According to local informants, the tank is filled with water only once a year, on the full moon day of Caitra during the celebration of a jātrā . When the procession cots stop in front of the Bālakūmāri Temple, water from the Capĩgāḥ is sprinkled on the cots. This Capĩgāḥ stands as an example of tangible and intangible heritage that has been severely affected by modern construction work.

label: Dune Bāhāḥ
description: Dune Bāhāḥ, a branch of Si Bāhāḥ ( LAL0690 ), is located to the west of the main Bāhāḥ and faces towards it also. Tall buildings surround the courtyard in which the building is located. The Bāhāḥ is also known as Bāhāḥcā, though its classical name is Duṇḍagṛha Bāhāḥ. Pruscha (1975, P-70) calls it Kaccā Bāhāḥ and Locke (1985, 174) mentions it as Bāchā Bāhāḥ. The ground floor sanctum is paved with stones and can be reached through a central door flanked by the statue of Gaṇeśa to the left and Mahākāla to the right. A stone statue of Prajñāpāramitā is attached to the wall above the entrance of the sanctum, and a stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum. The Bāhāḥ's carved door frames are its original ones, though the door leaves have been replaced with more simple framed metal shutters. The façade of the two-storey building is completely covered with cement plaster and a simple band of cornice marks the separate floors. Three small cement lattice windows have been placed asymmetrically on the first floor. Four plain struts support the overhanging corrugated metal sheet roof. Most of the original architecture of the building can no longer be found in this structure. A ś ikharakūṭa c aitya (130 cm high) is located at the centre of the courtyard, the base of which is covered by the raised stone flooring. No historical record with which one could date Bāhāḥ could be made available. Pruscha (P-70) suggests that it was built some time around the 17th century. In 1971, the Bāhāḥ was renovated and this was funded by selling a piece of its land. Śākyas are the saṅgha members of the Bāhāḥ; two families perform its daily ritual worships. The responsibility for this is passed on between families every 15 days.

label: Mahākāla Shrine (ca. early 20th cent. CE)
description: During special occasions such as jātrā and other festivities, the residents of Sunaguthi are supposed to worship four religious sites in the Sunaguthi area. This Mahākāla shrine is one of those four sites. On such occasions, long lines of devotees stand and queue in front of the shrine. The shrine contains a statue of Mahākāla (38 × 27 cm) and is located inside the south-facing shikhara -style temple. Mahākāla is standing on top of a corpse and holding kartikā , kapāl a and kha ṭvāṅga . A square stone pillar with a lotus pedestal on top of it stands to the west of the structure. This pillar was erected in 1951 (VS 2008) by Guru Kavi Prasada after he organised the saptāha bhajana in Sunaguthi. Next to it, a wooden post supports a small bell bearing an inscription from VS 2031 (1974 CE). A copper plate inscription can be found on the western wall of the shrine and states that the statue was restored in 2001 CE (VS 2058).

label: Mati Bāhācā (1863 CE)
description: Mati Bāhācā is a small courtyard containing two small monuments: one is a small shrine with Buddha’s image, and the other is a pañcāvaliyukta caitya . There is another courtyard is on the route leading from Naka Bahī to Dhalāyacā; one can cross through this to reach the Mati Bāhācā courtyard. This courtyard is not in fact a bahāḥ. Rather, it derives its name from Mati Bahā, and the fact that it is small in size. In 1863 CE (NS 983), Govinda Siṃha and his wife Vidyā Lakṣmī established a pañcāvaliyukta caitya inside the courtyard in memory of their son Jitamāna. After this, the courtyard began to be known as Govindasiṃha Vihāra. Local inhabitants also call this place Cibhāḥ Cuka. A p ancāvaliyukta caitya typically has five layers, consisting of images of lotuses, water, jewels, vajra and fire, and this one does not deviate from this structure. On the top of these layers ( āvali s) is the sanctum ( garbha ) of the Caitya. Below this garbha one can find images of Buddha at each of the four cardinal directions. Five small images of Lakhinarasiṃha, Jitamāna, Matiju, Govindasiṃha and Vidyā Thakuṃ have been engraved on the Caitya’s western plinth. There is an oil-lamp balustrade surrounding the Caitya, which spans over the RCC beams. These in turn are supported by short pillars. To the south of the Caitya is a small shrine made of stone with an image of Akṣobhya Buddha in its niche facing north. This shrine has been constructed on a plinth measuring 70 cm high and with a solid brick core. The Buddha image is housed in a smaller arched niche, also made of brick, which is covered by the stone slab roof of the stone temple. The stone temple structure itself measures 35 cm x 80 cm. The overall size of the temple is 150 cm x 120 cm, and it is 220 cm high. Its two-layered stone roof is decorated with lotus petals and crowned by a single ãvaḥsāḥ stone gajū. This in turn is backed by a brick masonry wall with a width equal to that of the stone temple. To the north of this shrine is a pañcāvali caitya constructed on a plinth measuring 150 cm high on a square base of 116 cm. There is also a newly established shrine for Sarasvatī near this shrine. This courtyard is accessible from Mati Bāhā (to the west) through a narrow opening demarcated by two carved columns that are 120 cm in height. This route is open during matayāḥ and other such festivals.

label: Vachẽ Nani Bāhāḥcā (1909 CE)
description: Vachẽ Nani Bāhāḥcā, a branch of Hakha Bāhāḥ ( LAL0390 ), is located behind the Haka Bāhāḥ and on the eastern side of a narrow street that goes from the Haka Bāhāḥ to Ikhālakhu. The bāhāḥcā is a small courtyard (7.2 m x 7.2 m) and can be accessed through another courtyard which is attached to the street. There is no kvaḥpāḥchẽ in this bāhāḥ . The main temple of the bāhāḥcā is built against the wall of a residential building facing west, and stands on a double plinth with a stone threshold. Timber lattice work surrounds the sanctum on three sides, whilst its rear wall is shared with the residential building. Inside, a statue of Akṣobhya has been placed on a high plinth so that it faces west. The roof is a two-tiered cement structure with a stone stūpa as its finial. A śikharakūṭotpannaparipadma caitya (187 cm high) can be found in front of the main temple structure at the centre of the courtyard. A statue of Gaṇeśa is located to the right of the temple and a statue of Hanumān can be found to its left. Both have been placed on the walls of the other buildings. This bāhāḥ was founded by Munirāja in 1909. The caitya was established prior to this in 1863, most likely by his father Dhanavantasiṃha Vajrācārya. This bāhāḥ is managed by three Vajrācārya families who are the descendants of Munirāja.

label: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
description: The single-storey Nārāyaṇa temple has a domed roof and is located on the eastern side of the road that runs north-south from Mangal Bazar to Lagankhel. The temple stands on a double plinth and can be accessed via stone steps to its west. The main arched entry is also to the west; blind stone doors can be found on the other three sides of the temple. There is a multi-layered terracotta motif above the entry level. A stone nāgo and floral ( libī ) motifl can be found almost half way up the temple, in between the layer and the base. All the doors are topped with kīrtimukha toraṇas. A stone image of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu stands in the sanctum in a samapāda posture, holding śaṅkha and cakra in his two right hands, and gadā and padma in his left hands. Images of Lakṣmī and Garuḍa have been sculpted on the same stone. Lakṣmī stands to the left of Viṣṇu in tribhaṅga. Her left hand is shown performing a gesture of abhaya whilst her right hand performs varada . Garuḍa stands to Viṣṇu's right in samapāda, and is in a praying posture. Images of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu usually show Lakṣmī to his right and Garuḍa on his left. However, in this statue their position has been inverted. In addition to this main statue, there is also a smaller and partially damaged image of Viṣṇu in the sanctum. This has been placed inside a niche. The rectangular base of the bell-shaped dome has a number of niches containing idols of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. These can be found on all four sides. A bronze pinnacle sits on top of the temple. Recently (in 2012), a wind vane was fixed next to the pinnacle, alongside statues of Viṣṇu's weapons. An oil-lamp balustrade with 108 lamps surrounds the temple, while a bell donated on the same date hangs on a beam besides the lower plinth at its southwest corner. A pillar with an image showing Garuḍa sitting and praying to Śrīdhara Viṣṇu was also erected in 2012. No inscription mentioning the exact date of the establishment of the temple could be found. However, an astrologer called Śivanārāyaṇa installed a stone inscription dated NS 819 inside the temple. This stone records the names of his predecessors, and provides grounds to hypothesise that either he or one of them established the temple. Inside the sanctum, another broken inscription dated NS 754 informs readers of the renovation of a phalcā , which suggests that this inscription was brought here from somewhere else. The daily and annual ritual worships of this temple are no longer performed. The Cakravarti Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti organises the opening and closing of the temple.

label: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ (built around seventeenth and eighteenth century)
description: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ is one of the numerous small temples built in the Bāghabhairava Temple Complex ( KIR0004 ). A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum of this Degaḥ, and there is also one other Śivaliṅga in the sanctum. There is no evidence to date the initial construction of the temple. However, a careful study of its wooden elements suggests that the temple might have been built around seventeenth and eighteenth century. A sketch of the temple drawn by Henry Ambrose Oldfield around 1855 CE shows it in ruins with both roofs damaged completely. It is probable that the temple suffered severe damages during the 1832 CE earthquakes and was not renovated till 1850s. In the same sketch, a tora ṇ a can be seen crowning the temples's western door, which it does not exist in the present-day. In the Rāṇā Period, the temple was reconstructed with a domed roof. It was dismantled and reconstructed as a tiered temple again in 1999 CE (VS 2056) (local knowledge, a local resident, Maharjana, male, age 53). An inscription from 1844 CE (NS 964) is installed on the southern wall of the temple. It mentions that a phalcā was constructed around the place of Yamaleśvara, and reminds the members of the gu ṭhī about their obligations and duties. The phalcā is not related to the temple. On the basis of this inscription, Ś. Śre ṣṭ ha (VS 2057, 44) named this temple as Yamaleśvara Mandira. There is no guthi associated with Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ. Even elders of the local community cannot recall any gu ṭhī or any social or religious activities associated with the temple. A group of local youth lights up a bonfire on the day of Śivarātrī in front of the temple.

label: Naḥ Bāhāḥcā (before 1548 CE)
description: Naḥ Bāhāḥcā is one of the branches of Si Bāhāḥ ( LAL0690 ) and is located at the south-west corner of the largest courtyard of Naḥ Bāhāḥ Nani. One can reach the bāhāḥcā via a narrow underpass from the south-west corner of the nani . The two-storey building faces east, and an aṣṭakoṇoparipadma caitya stands in front of its sanctum. The principal façade of the monument building has a carved wooden door at its centre flanked by two small lattice windows. There is no toraṇa but small images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara surmounted by a small caitya image have been fixed to the lintel above the door. Two small niches made from wooden frames also flank the sanctum entrance. Stone statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been placed in the niches to the left and right respectively. The front wall of the first storey has been separated into three sections. One part contains the sanctum door, one part has a Gaṇeśa statue and the third part holds a Bhairava statue. The joint line between these sections is clearly visible. A band of carved wooden cornice separates the first floor from the second floor. The façade of the first floor largely consists of an intricately carved three bay window ( pasukājhyāḥ ) which is flanked by two small blind windows. The remaining wall area has been painted white. Figures of Namasaṅgīti and Amoghapāśa are displayed on either side of the window, whilst images of the Seven Buddhas can be seen above the window. The roof of the god house is made from corrugated metal sheets and supported by plain struts. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined inside the sanctum. The literal meaning of Naḥ Bāhāḥ is ‘a new monastic building’. Recently, the monastic building located at the north-east corner of this small monastic building was known as Naḥ Bāhāḥ. However, locals claim that this Naḥ Bāhāḥcā (LAL0530) is the original Naḥ Bāhāḥ. In earlier times, a pond called Khāsāpukhū was located to the north west of this bāhāḥcā . However, the pond has since been filled in and a school named Svatantra Śikṣā Sadana runs this area. The bāhāḥcā was given its classical name, Yokulivarṇa Mahāvihāra, due to its proximity to the pond; yokuli means 'north-western direction' in the Nevārī language. No sources could be found with which to date the initial construction of this bāhāḥcā . Pruscha 1975 (1975, C/P-53) dates this monument to the 17th century and mentions that it was renovated by a guṭhī in 1933, though he does not provide evidence to support this claim. A palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 688 (1548 CE) makes mention of a monastic building named Naka Bāhāra. It could be that this refers to the present monument. Long ago, most of the saṅgha members of the bāhāḥcā were Śākyas who were carpenters by occupation. Locke (1985: 178) mentions that the last surviving male member of this household died without any sons. Afterwards, the husbands of his daughters inherited the rights, duties and properties of their father-in-law. Later, these families stopped performing social and religious activities in the bāhāḥcā . At present, four families affiliated with the Āagama Guṭhī of the Naḥ Bāhāḥ Nani perform daily ritual worships in the bāhāḥcā . When cuḍākaraṇa (shaving one's hair for the first time), initiations, jaṃko and other rituals are organised in the Si Bāhāḥ, these people also come to visit this bāhāḥcā .

label: Tāpā Hiti Sataḥ
description: The two-storey Sataḥ faces towards the east. No historical record is available to date the building. Villagers from Tamang and Magar communities would stay overnight in this Sataḥ when they came to the Valley to sell their local products, though this no longer seems to be the case. Ekatā Paṭhaśālā was established in the building during the Rana period. Afterwards, the building was used by the Ganesh Youth Club, and the first floor of the building was also used by the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti. The office was moved to a new building constructed on top of the filled in pond to the north of Tāpā Hiti Phalcā East ( LAL4199 ). This likely occured some time in the 2010s. At present, the ground floor of the Sataḥ is used to store old materials. The sataḥ building has been deteriorating over time and was further damaged by the earthquakes of 2015. The inner walls of the building have cracked in many places.

label: Buramāṃ Vaidya Bāhāḥ (1866 CE)
description: The Buramāṃ Vaidya Bāhāḥ is a branch of Cikã Bahī ( LAL1620 ) and lies to its north. The courtyard is surrounded by residential housing and can be entered through the gates of a private house. The dyaḥchẽ (god house) is located on the south of the courtyard with its sanctum on the ground floor. An oil-lamp balustrade is fixed on the plinth of the dyaḥchẽ . A torana above the entrance displays Buddha, Nāmasaṅgīti and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara. The sanctum's carved central door is flanked by plain lattice windows and small statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been placed in the ground floor wall niches. In the sanctum statues of Buddha, Nāmasaṅgīti and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara rest on stone pedestals. A statue of Mañjuśrī is enshrined inside a room to the right of the sanctum and a statue of Vasundharā resides in the room to the left of the sanctum. The houses on the west and north sides of the courtyard are built in traditional Newar style with colonnaded ground floors and carved triple-bay windows on their first and second floors. These openings have cusped arches and can be dated to the early Saha period. Both houses have two new additional floors on top. The house on the east has been completely rebuilt in modern style. According to a local resident, all of the houses were once owned by the same family and used to be interconnected, however, they were later divided among the brothers. The surfaces of these houses are a particularly interesting feature of this courtyard. Each of the plastered surfaces of the walls facing into the courtyard has been decorated with wall paintings. The surfaces seem to have been made from a mixture of mud, rice husk and cow dung. Some of the wall paintings depict various deities, while others (such as the wall of the western corner of the god-house) are covered in verses in Sanskrit, most probably excerpts from the Jātaka tales (see photo: LAL1630_I_20191006_01). Most of the painted surfaces have eroded and only a few traces of the paintings remain intact today. A photo printed in Locke (1985, 213) shows that the house on the eastern side also had similar paintings and windows, however since its reconstruction it no longer has these features. On the wall paintings are depictions of various deities, some from Jātaka tales, Locke (1985, 214) maintains that the Bāhāḥ was founded in NS 986 (1866 CE) without providing a source. A stone inscription on the vedi of the northern face of the dharmadhātu jinālaya caitya mentions that Maṇiratna Vaidya enshrined the images of Triratnas in the sanctum in NS 998. Three days afterwards, the naming ceremony of the monastic building took place, where it was given the name "Maṇikūṭa Vihāra". The families affiliated with the guṭhī of the monastic building were professional vaidya s (practitioners of Ayurvedic medicine); the monastic building is therefore also known as Vaidya Bāhāḥ.

label: Taḥgaḥcībhāḥ ca. 16th cent.
description: Taḥgaḥcībhāḥ Caitya ("Big Caitya") is located at the south-west corner of Macchindrabāhāḥ. It is the biggest caitya in this area and exhibits a style typical of the 16th century ( Gutschow (2011, vol 1: 152). H. Śākya (1993, 82) describes it as a Vajradhātu caitya . The caitya is built with small traditional mā apā bricks which attests to its antiquity. The four corners, the frames around the niches and the finial are all made of stone. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi are installed in the eastern, southern, western and northern niches of the caitya respectively. In addition, a statue of Akṣobhya is attached to the eastern plinth and an inscription has been placed on the south-eastern corner of the caitya . The inscription mentions that the caitya was renovated by five Śākyas in 1749 CE. A historical photo from 2000 (published in Bu ṅgamatīko Sā̃skṛtika Sampadāharū , p. 50) shows that the caitya was in a dilapidated condition. However, it was renovated in 2002. A Śākya family residing in the vicinity south of the caitya takes care of it and performs all annual rituals.

label: Garuḍa Stambha (1637 CE)
description: In 1637, King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla built this pillar in collaboration with the Kṛṣṇa Temple ( LAL1340 ). The gilded Garuḍa statue stands on an almost 7 meter tall rectangular pillar, measuring 55 x 55 cm. The 171 cm tall statue is greeting Kṛṣṇa in namaskāra gestur, and sits on a pedastal decorated with lotus petals. Whenever Kṛṣṇa is worshipped in the temple, the statue also receives some of the pūjā material, as Garuḍa is the vehicle of Viṣṇu. The image is therianthropic; half of it is in the shape of a bird, while the other half has a human appearance. Garuḍa appears in a benign posture; he is kneeling with his right knee upwards and his left knee on the pedastal as he prays to Kṛṣṇa. He is wearing a crown, and has a red ṭīkā on his forehead. Snakes adorn his neck and ears as ornaments, and he wears armlets on his wrists and arms. He has dhotī on his lower body and a girdle on his waist. Two wings and a tail can be found on his back.

label: Guitaḥ Caitya 2
description: Guitaḥ Caitya 2 is located to the east of the Cīdhã Bahī ( LAL1970 ) and to the north of the Guitaḥ Hiti. It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the four cardinal directions. The platform is paved with teliā tiles and has a stone edge. A fire alter can be found in the courtyard in front of the shrine. The main deity is Akṣobhya and his statue has been placed in the western niche. This is unusual, as he is normally located on the eastern side of such caitya. Here, however, he faces towards the main deity in the Cīdhã Bahī. This main western niche is adorned with a stone doorframe displaying images of the Five Buddhas. The other three niches are plain and exhibit a different type of roof. The diameter of the single-plinth drum is 790 cm and the dome atop it has a diameter of 720 cm. Above the dome is a harmikā based on a square plan of 187 cm and measuring 100 cm in height. There are thirteen rectangular tiers and an āmalaka and a yaḥsĩ (central pillar) above the harmikā, and a gilded parasol has been fixed above the caitya . A statue of Ratnasambhava undeneath five nāgas (snakes) is housed in the southern niche of the Caitya. These five nāgas intertwine to form a triangular shape above him. Amitābha is enshrined in the eastern niche and Amoghasiddhi is located in the northern one. The images of Amitābha and Ratnasambhava seem to be have been added recently. These four shrines have been topped with caitya -shaped pinnacles, though the pinnacle of the northern niche is damaged. The main Caitya is surrounded by four smaller khaṭa- style caityas at its four corners; this formation is known as cila ̃dyaḥ. These caityas have been painted with white lime and house images of Buddha. Images of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara have been enshrined inside the north-western and north-eastern caityas . An image of a six-handed deity standing on a yoni has been enshrined in the south-eastern caitya . The deity’s face, as well as the number of his hands and weapons cannot be seen clearly. He might be one of the Lokeśvaras. Inside the south-western khaṭa -shaped caitya, one can find a sitting statue of Vairocana alongside his associative deities. L. Bangdel (1995, 228) has dated the Vairocana image to around the 6th century. All four caitya s have small caitya shaped pinnacles at their top. The pinnacles of the north-western and south-eastern structures have been damaged; only the āmalaka part of the remains. The thirteen tiers of the north-eastern caitya have also been lost. No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide information about the establishment of the caitya . Since the Vairocana image on the south-western khaṭa -shaped caitya has been dated to the 6th century, it can be assumed that the main Caitya was also constructed around that time.

label: Śaṅkhadhara Bāhāḥ (1868 CE)
description: Śaṅkhadhara Bāhāḥ is an independent vihāra . The building is located on the right-hand side of the street that leads from Bhelāchẽ to Cyāsal Square, and is easily identifiable thanks to the three phalcās that surround it. One phalcā sits in front of the monument (to the west), the second is attached to the southern side of the building, and the third can be found to its north just across the street. The Bāhāḥ sits on a high plinth of 75 cm; this has been built using unusually large bricks. The decorative kasimvaḥ and libī bricks are also larger than is characteristic for a bāhāḥ . The sanctum can be accessed by climbing a series of steps that are flanked by two stone lions. The building has a single carved door on the ground floor of the main facade, which faces west. The door is guarded by a pair of terracotta serpents with a decorative brick lining. The upper floor is separated by a band of timber cornices with a pair of lhāḥkā at each of their projected ends. On the first floor, a carved window is set in the center of the main wall and has two small blind windows on either sides. The original struts, the toraṇa and the roof structure are all missing. A new floor has been built on top of the first floor using brick masonry and mud mortar. This floor has a double-leaf glazed window. The building is now covered in corrugated metal sheets. The front yard is paved in stone. It has a caitya (225 cm high) on a square brick base and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala lined up on its western axis. This independent vihāra was established by Śaṅkhadhara Prajāpati in 1868 (NS 988). The carved, brass entrance of the sanctum has no toraṇa, but it does have the usual two stone lions sitting in front of it. The main image of Akṣobhya has been lost, and since then the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ has remained empty. A photo printed in Pruscha (1975, 176) shows stone pillars erected on the left-hand side of the plinth. These pillars are meant to hold a bell, however this too is missing. The pillars are also no longer there. To the left of the entrance, a small image of a four-handed Gaṇeśa has been placed in a small niche in the wall. Below this image, a stone inscription informs readers of the establishment of the Bāhāḥ. To the right of the entrance, one can find a small iamge of Kumāra riding on a peacock. An inscription mentions that Śaṅkhadhara Prajāpati established a guṭhī and provided it with land for the management of this Bāhāḥ. These days, however, the Bāhāḥ seems to be somewhat neglected. The ritual worship is also no longer performed.

label: Gaddi Baithak
Bāsimali Phalcā (1868 CE)
description: Bāsimali Phalcā is located to the northwest of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and lies between Dhvākhā Phalcā and Āratī Chẽ. There are more than half a dozen phalcās in the courtyard of this temple. Many of the social-cultural activities related to Karuṇāmaya are organised in the locality, and these phalcās were constructed as sites within which to hold such activities. This three-bayed phalcā is located on the ground floor of a three-storey building. The roof of the building is supported by six carved struts and is covered with corrugated metal sheets. The second storey has a three-bayed window. The construction of this phalcā was facilitated by a Tāmrākāra family from Cāsukhela, Bhaktapur in 1868 CE. Originally, the building was called satala. Its founders had established a guṭhī for its management. However, the building collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was reconstructed by the desecendents of the founders in 1942. A historical photo taken around 1968 shows that the building once had a jhĩgaṭī -tiled roof and a traditional window ( Bungamati 1968, 21). The Bāsimali Phalcā collapsed again in 2001 and in the same year Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra, another descendent of the founders, took on the task of renovating it. Once the renovations were complete, she deposited a lump sum of money in the bank to allow for the continuation and management of bhajana chanting in Bāsimali Phalcā. A statue of Vāsuki Nāga and a lion are attached to the inner wall of the phalcā . Locals worship Vāsuki as Viṣṇu and the lion as Garuḍa. Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra also donated musical instruments to a bhajana group in 2001, and this group now performs bhajana during the months of Gũlā and Kārttika. A group of yogin returns here after taking part in the Hariśaṅkara procession of Pharping before proceeding on to the Paśupatinātha Temple to perform Jogīcakra Pūjā. Upon returning from Pharping, the yogins carry a thick roṭī on their head which is tied and fixed in place by knots made by their matted hair. They rest for a while in Bāsimali Phalcā and offer the roṭīs to Karuṇāmaya. Afterwards, they distribute the remaining roṭī to the public as the gift of the deity. Some of the locals claim that the stale mali (Nep. ro ṭī ) was distributed in the phalcā, and that this is how the monument got its name.

Kvāḥcva Khyālidyaḥ Phalcā
description: This non-existing rest house was constructed by a person named Dharaṇīdhara in 1694 CE (NS 814). Only a small shrine of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa remains at the center of the square pavilion where the Phalcā once stood. The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa faces west towards Umāmaheśvara Mandira ( KIR0006 ) while the inscription recording the construction of the Phalcā is set on the rear wall of the shrine. The inscription states that Dharaṇīdhara, who constructed the Phalcā in 1694 CE, was a resident of Kirtipur and held the post of the chief of the fort. The fort probably is a reference to the city of Kirtipur. It further mentions that the Phalcā’s architecture was similar to Kaṣṭhamaṇḍapa of Kathmandu. The donor also endowed seven ropanī s of land to form a guthi for performing various rituals throughout the year ( Shokoohy and others 2014, p. 94). The Phalcā is due to be reconstructed in traditional architecture with funds from the US embassy. The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa exudes the emotion of love, as the four-armed Nārāyaṇa is seen in amorous disposition, embracing his consort Lakṣmī while slightly bending towards her. Locals, therefore, call the deity ‘Khyālidyaḥ’, the deity of love. There is a local belief that worshipping Khyālidyaḥ brings the person’s love affair to a successful conclusion. The inscription also instructs concerned persons to organize the hāthu hāyke tradition. This proves that the tradition of discharging fermented beer ( thvã ) from the Bhairava mask (Hāthudyaḥ) existed here. This tradition is no longer in practice.

label: Bhailaḥsĩ Bāhāḥ (1896 CE)
description: Bhailaḥsĩ Bāhāḥ, a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ ( LAL0440 ), can be reached via a narrow alley at the north-east corner of Bu Bāhāḥ and by passing through two small courtyards. This four-storey bāhāḥ stands in the north-west corner of its courtyard (10 m x 12 m). A statue of Akṣobhya facing east is enshrined in the main sanctum, which is located on the ground floor and can be reached by climbing the stairs of a three bayed phalcā with a front row of columns. The central bay of this structure is surmounted by a carved tora ṇa showing images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara. A painting of Buddhist images can be found on the mud plaster wall of the bāhāḥ's first floor. This level is also decorated with a lattice window flanked by two oval Tibetan-style paintings of Buddha‘s birth. A three-bayed window covers the principal façade on the third floor. An fourth floor has been added above the original floors, and now houses the āgama deity of the bāhā ḥ. A private house to the north of the bāhāḥ exhiits similar Tibetan-style images of Caturmahārāja painted on oval mud plaster. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala (85 cm high) is located in front of the bāhāḥ and a śikharakūṭa caitya (165 cm high) can be found at the center of the courtyard. There are three exits at the east, north-east, and south-east corners. This bāhāḥ was established in 1896 (NS 1016) and is named after its founder, Bhairavasiṃha Vajrācārya.

label: Bhaiṣajyarāja Bāhāḥ (1878 CE)
description: Bhaiṣajyarāja Bāhāḥ, a branch of the Cikã Bahī (Saptapura Mahāvihāra, LAL1620 ), is located behind a five-bayed phalcā at the junction of the street from Bhelāchẽ and Bhindyaḥ Sataḥ at Cyāsal. The entrance to this Bāhāḥ is on a boundary wall to the west and it is attached to a phalcā to its south. The main structure is divided into three small rooms, consisting of a central sanctum room and two small rooms on either side. A small staircase in the eastern room leads up to the upper floor. The building shares a small space with a single-storey annex structure to its north. The courtyard measures 7 m × 4.7 m, and has a residential building to the its east and north. Both of these are built on arcaded phalcās that serve as the ground floor. A caitya sits to the north of the Bāhāḥ, directly in front of its main door. The courtyard is paved with telia tiles. Small images of different Buddhist deities have been placed on the walls of the southern annex building and western boundary wall. Jīvanṛsiṃha, a member of the Cikã Bahī and an Āyurvedic doctor (vaidya) by profession, established this Bāhāḥ in 1878 (NS 998). It takes its name from Jīvanṛsiṃha's profession; hence, it is known as Bhaiṣajyarāja Bāhāḥ. Wall paintings of the Five Buddhas can be found above the plain outer entrance , which is flanked by paintings of auspicious symbols. The north-facing god house has two storeys and a tiled roof supported by plain struts. Instead of a pinnacle, a small chimney ( bhaipvāḥ ) can be found on its sloping roof, as well as three metal banners displaying images of deities. The first floor of the god house is very low. There is no toraṇa above the carved door of the sanctum, though it is flanked by two stone lions as it is customary. The lions also sit next to two metal flags that were donated in 1909 (NS 1023). The main facade of the god-house was decorated with wall paintings of various deities, but the old plaster is now crumbling away, making most of the paintings unrecognizable. Inside the sanctum, one can find a north-facing stone image of Akṣobhya.

label: Gãdyaḥ Phalcā
description: The Gãdyaḥ Phalcā is located at Pukhusi, Sunaguthi (widely known as Sunakothi) at the junction where a street leading towards Kulimha curves away from the Sunāguthi main road. No evidence could so far be traced with which to date the initial construction of this Phalcā. The photo published in Pruscha 1975 (vol. 1), 99 shows the building's original structure before it was rebuilt in 1995 due to damage suffered by its earlier five-bayed structure. The reconstruction saw the addition of a blank masonry wall to the rear and eastern sides. The Phalcā is open to the south and west directions, though it is protected by a grill. Two small metal doors are fixed to the southern wall. The foundation stone of the old structure can be seen on the plinth, and some of the salvaged roof tiles are stacked on top of the roof slab. The Phalcā has socio-cultural importance for Patan. The masks of the Navadurgās from Thecva are stored here during the Mohanī festival before they are taken to way to (and return from) a performance at Mūla Coka ( LAL1260 ) at Patan Darbar Square. Local residents come here to worship the masks and take part in a procession around Sunaguthi. The procession is followed by a dance performance in front of Kvaylāchī Phalcā ( SUN4200 ).

label: Ghana Bāhāḥ (ca. 1840 CE)
description: Ghana Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260 ), is a small area surrounded by a historic, private building to the north, the Mahākāla Phalcā to the east, the Vajradhara Phalcā to the west and small buildings and a boundary wall to the south. Ghanānanda Śākya, a grandson of Amṛtānanda Vande (the man who taught Buddhism to Brian Hodgson), established this bāhāḥ and it is from him that it gets its name. The small, single-roofed domed shrine is made of bricks and contains a stone image of Akṣobhya in its sanctum. Akṣobhya is facing west, and there is a rounded dharmadhātu maṇḍala in front of him. The shrine itself is located between the two phalcā s and rests on a single plinth. Parts of the base and the dome have been plastered with lime and white-washed, and the walls are built of daci apa and decorative bricks. The stone doorway features an arch with the Five Buddhas carved on it. A well can be found to the south of the shrine. No historical document could be found to provide the exact date the bāhāḥ was constructed. However, it is possible to estimate a rough date with the help of sources that tell us about Ghanānanda's life more generally. Ghanānanda is mentioned in an inscription dated NS 955 ( Śākya 1994, 55-56). Furthermore, in NS 975 (1855 CE), on the first anniversary of his death, a dharmadhātu maṇḍala was established in front of the Mahābuddha Temple ( LAL2340 ) in his honour ( Śākya 1988, 88-89) . This suggests that the bāhāḥ was established before 1854 and very probably after 1835.

label: Licchavi Caitya (9th century)
description: This Licchavi caitya is located to the north of the street that leads to Karuṇamaya Temple ( BUN0001 ) just after passing the Dey Pukhu. It is built on top of a square base measuring 90 x 90 cm and with total height of 145 cm. Only the upper part of the caitya seems to be from the original Licchavi structure. Stone slabs have been placed aroud the base of the caitya, forming a roof-like form over the square base and the stone statues in its walls. H. Śā kya (1993, 72) refers to this monument as Caturdvāreṣu Caityāṅkita Caitya. A few decades ago, a functioning hiti (stone spout) could be found to the east of the Gaṇeśa Mandira (BUN0025) of the Kotā Ṭola. Later, water stopped flowing from the spout and it fell into disuse. Now, the area is full of refuse, and the spout area has been covered with mud. Before it was filled in, a Licchavi period caitya , a statue of Bhagīratha, the original spout and some other statues were moved away from the hiti to their present locations. Bhagīratha’s statue and the spout have been fixed to the new hiti, which is located in front of the Gaṇeśa Mandira. Bangdel (1995, 358) dates the Bhagīratha statue to the 9th century. A statue of Umāmaheśvara (which is dated by Bangdel (1995, 357) to the 9th century) has been placed on the western side of the present caitya . Its western niche remains empty. According to local residents, there was a statue of Nārāyaṇa in the niche. However, this was stolen around 1994. The northern niche of the caitya has a deteriorated statue which is thought to be Śivapārvatī. A Licchavi caitya has been joined to the upper part of the Caturdvāreṣu Caityāṅkita Caitya. The upper caitya has small caitya -shaped objects in its four niches. The garbha has been damaged in many places, and has been joined to the niche and the harmikās with cement. To the east of this caitya, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya which was established here in 1956. Local residents worship this caitya whilst visiting other shrines in the morning.

label: Tāhā Phalcā
description: Tāhā Phalcā is located to the north-east of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ). It derives its name from the Newari term ‘ t āhā ’ , which means “long”. It was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, which led to it being dismantled and reconstructed in 2017. The five-bayed Phalcā has six carved wooden posts. Two-thirds of the building have a flat slab roof whilst the remaining part is covered by a hip roof tiled with traditional pvala apā . Thirty-seven struts have been fixed in place to support the roof. The walls of the building are made of desi apā (modern bricks). There are four latticed windows on the first floor and seven on the second floor. Tāhā Phalcā is used to organise many social-cultural activities related to the deity. During the months of Guṃlā and Kārttika, various groups from Bungmati come to chant bhajanas in the Phalcā. The Jyāpu community from Lāchi Ṭola are particularly common amongst the chanters who visit this Phalcā. The upper storey of the building is mostly used to organise feasts, though many other social gatherings are also organised in its rooms.

label: Kumbheśvara/Konti (कुम्भेश्वर/कोन्ति)
Lagankhel/Lagãkhyaḥ (लगनखेल/लगँख्यः)
Guita (गुइत)
Pimbahal
description: Like Cyāsal, Pimbahal has a vibrant political and cultural history and life that also manifests in its larger ensemble of monuments, and intangible heritage, and turns it into one of the relevant monument zones we have defined (please note that by doing so, we do not follow official and administrative boundaries!). Pimbahal is a unique part of Patan’s urban heritage and dynamic life, with a high condensation of sites used for social, religious, economic and cultural purposes. For this case study on DANAM, we have documented 12 phalcās and six other heritage monuments, ranging from monastic compound to shrine and temple Similar to the Cyāsal case, too, Pimbahal’s built heritage was also affected by the Gorkha earthquakes of 2015. Both use their open spaces, one of the few larger ones in the otherwise condensed network of Old Patan, intensively. Pimbahal area and sites were quickly regenerated and got a ‘facelift’ that has pushed the open space around the famous pond into a popular site for both local residents and other visitors. As in the case of Cyāsal, Pimbahal locality is made up of various castes: Śreṣṭhas, Rājopādhyāyas (Newark Brahmins), Maharjanas (farmers), Śākyas, , Kapālīs (Newar musicians and caretaker of the temples) and Bhāratīs (Daśanāmī Sanyāsīs), for instance. The associations related to the area have started to revitalize some of their ritual and other cultural practices. Pimbahal and Cyāsal share their open squares and engaged socio-cultural activities as well as historic Cila͂ (possibly Ashokan, 250 BCE) Caitya. There is also a three storied medieval pagoda temple of Caṇḍeśvarī towards the northern side of the pond, the lineage deity of Pātravaṃśa Śreṣṭhas of this area. Another strong association, the to Digvijaya's Lākhe clan, is to the Lākhe (lit. 'demon'), and some representatives of the Pātravaṃśa Śreṣṭha clan promite this association, also through rejuvenation of related rituals in this particular vicinity. The pond is believed to have been made by Lākhes (either clan members or the premodern figure of the Lākhe demon), following the order of Gayo Brahman/Bāje. [1] All four sub-clans claim that they once migrated from Banepa, a small historical town located to east of the Kathmandu Valley. Each clan also celebrates annual linage deity worship once a year jointly and separately as well in the temple of Caṇḍeśvarī. The social topography around the pond contains many legends related to the famous tantric Gayo Bāje and the lineage goddess Caṇḍeśvarī. During the annual festival of Indrajātrā, figures of Yamadyaḥ (Indra) are displayed in many phalcās and samay-baji (ritual food with 5 kinds of edible things like beaten rice, buffalo meat, vegetable etc.) is distributed as prasāda by the donor or guṭhīyāra family of the sites . One also finds worship of other deities, gurus and ancestors in several phalcās , edcative, social and religious activities. Local and municipality organisations have actively engaged in post-earthquake reconstruction of damaged sites around Pimbahal, Chāybahal and Sulima areas. The Jagamadu Pukhu Kṣetra Vikāsa Samiti (Jagamadu Pond Area Development Committee), in collaboration with Lalitpur Metropolitan office and World Bank, implemented the Pimbahal Pond Repair Project (almost 6 lakh Rs.), a Project for Stone Paving around the Pond area (almost 6 lakh Rs.) and a Rainwater Harvesting Project (almost 5 lakh Rs.) in 2017.

label: Cyāsal (च्यासल्)
description: Cyāsal is one of the key monument heritage areas selected for the NHDP pilot phase (please note that by doing so, we neither follow the official and administrative boundaries, such as defined by the Department of Archeology, nor do we intend to create a new heritage zone that collide with the existing official boundaries!). It is a unique site, of various interconnected and meandering squares that turn Cyasal also into one of the few large open areas the densely built old city of Patan has (other exceptions are Pimbahal and Patan Darbar Square, see monument areas…). The area is very popular among local residents and urban youth from the Kathmandu Valley as well as some tourists. Especially the festivals are popular, but the area also has some remarkable smaller and larger monuments that deserve our attention. As an ensemble, Cyāsal tole (Ṭola) is, thus, a remarkable habitat of both Newar urban cultural heritage and modern facets interrelated. The ancient trade-route cutting through the square from East to West, is still relevant. Cyāsal is now surrounded by splintering urbanism, most fields have been sold and converted into ground for constructions. For NHDP, we have so far documented 20 phalcās and in this small-scale vicinity, which has a density of public and semi-public monuments as hardly any other neighbourhood in Patan’s old city, possibly even Kathmandu. Moreover, eight other monuments such as shrines, ponds/stepwells, caitya / stūpas and monasteries have been documented and mapped. Although Cyāsal’s buildings, residential and public, were quite badly hit by the earthquakes of 2015, reconstruction was very important, also because residents of the area are proud of the tangible and intangible heritage and actively use and engage in practicing it, be it for festivals, feasts, annual rituals and processions, or devotional chanting. The locality has got several Licchavi period stone inscriptions to trace back its history to ancient period. Also, one of the four Cila͂caityas believed to be built about 2250 years ago during the time of Great King Aśoka of Magadh (India) is also situated here. The shadow play in the Bhailaḥ (Avaḥ Guṭhī) capāḥ during Indrajātrā is the cultural specialty of this area. Cyāsal was a final battlefield for the battle between Kirantas and Lichhavis. About 250 A.D., Lichhavis are said to have attacked this post, killing 800 Kirantas who were guarding the post. In Newari language, 800 means chyasa , thus this place is also a ‘memory site’. Mainly people from the caste of the “Vyan͂janakāra” (traditionally kitchen gardeners) and Avāle (often tilers, potters) reside here, the latter more towards the South of the large square, the first towards the North. Earlier, there would have been communal tensions between these groups, but those have now become part of the folkloristic memory rather than active conflict. Members of Maharjan farmers, members of Śākya or Śhreṣṭha castes also live in and around Cyāsal square. According to an Avāle resident (aged 55) the Avāles are divided into two guṭhī s i. e. the Cidha͂ (smaller) and the Tadha͂ (bigger) and into ten Si (death) Guṭhīs as well. The members of Cidha͂ Guṭhī are called Lā manaṃ (vegetarians). Only five families still live in Bhindyaḥlāchi. The other Avāles are connected to the Tadha͂ Guṭhī. Some Avāles have migrated from Kathmandu, near Ason Tole (Asana Ṭola), to Cyāsal Tole. They shifted their lineage deity from Lainchaur to Depacākhyaḥ in Shankhamool (Śaṅkhamūla), Patan and worship her in the month of Pauṣa/Māgha (Jan-March).

label: Nagbahal/Nāga Bāhāḥ (नाग्बाहाल्/नाग बाहाः)
Tāpā Hiti (तापा हिति)
Pulchok/Pūcvā (पुल्चोक/पूच्वा)
Taṅgala (तङ्गल)
Buṅgamatī (बुङ्गमती)
description: Located south of Patan, Bungamati is an important settlement for intangible and tangible heritage. The predominantly Newar town’s historical core has been heavily damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. Nearly two thirds of the houses have been damaged or destroyed, many heritage monuments collapsed or are still endangered, including the temple of the main deity.

label: Sundhara/Lũhiti/Nugaḥ (सुन्धारा/लुँहिति/नुगः)
Bālakumarī (बालकुमारी)
Okubahal/Oku Bāhāḥ (ओकुबहाल/ओकु बाहाः)
Patan Darbar Square/Mangal Bazar (पाटन दरबार परिसर/मङ्गल बजार)
description: Patan Durbar Square is the heart of the old town of Lalitpur and one of three royal squares in the Kathmandu Valley, all of which are declared UNESCO World Heritage Sites. One of its attractions is the ancient Royal Palace where the Malla Kings of Lalitpur resided. NHDP has documented many previously undocumented monuments located at this Square.

label: Sunakothi/Sunāguthi (सुनकोथि/सुनागुथि)
description: The Newar settlement of Sunaguthi, located c. 6 km south of Patan, is remarkably rich in its largely undocumented tangible and intangible heritage. Particularly the attempt to widen the main road where many of the heritage sites lie, has led to their extremely endangered status. NHDP has documented most of hose vulnerable sites.

label: Khaḍācakra Koṭa Darbar (खडाचक्र कोत दरबार)
Kirtipur (कीर्तिपुर)
description: Kirtipur, an old Newar settlement of the Kathmandu Valley is believed to be founded by King Sadāśivadeva (ca. 1099-1126 CE). The citizens of this ancient Newar city have engaged in preserving the rich tangible and intangible heritage sites that have been included in the ‘World Heritage List Nominations’ by UNESCO. The city, with its numerous temples, stūpas, caityas or arcaded platforms, dynamised by several impressive processions, festivals and other cultural activities, is a remarkable repository of cultural heritage from Nepal. Kirtipur hosts the unique Bāghabhairava temple, Cilincva Caitya and Umāmaheśvara temple.

label: Bhurti Temple Complex
description: The Bhurtī temple complex is located 3 km north of Nārāyaṇa, the Dailekh district headquarter. It currently comprises 22 standing śikhara temples (or devala ) and one stone fountain. Architectural activity at the site can be situated between the 13 th and 15 th century, a time period corresponding to the latter part of the Khaśa Malla empire and the early phase of the Rāskoṭi dynasty. In 2008, the “Bhurti Temple Complex of Dailekh” was enlisted on UNESCO’s World Heritage Tentative List by the Government of Nepal (criteria ii and iv).

label: LAL1730_I_001 A pedestal inscription at Cī Bāhāḥ Nani, Olakhu Ṭola, Lalitpur
Vāsaḥ Hiti
description: Basaḥ Hiti is one of three hitis located next to each other at the base of the Imūdvã hillock in Lalitpur. The neighborhood is mainly inhabited by the members of Poḍe caste who . Therefore, the hiti is commonly used by them. The term vāsa ḥ means medicine in the Newari language, and thus, it is believed that water from this hiti contains medicinal properties. It is said that the Rāṇā rulers used to drink water from the Vāṣah Hiti ( Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 42). The hiti has two water spouts. A statue of Bhagīratha is installed underneath the main spout (LAL0994-001) and a statue of Umāmaheśvara is placed above it. The date of construction of the hiti is not recorded but it is assumed that it was built during the reign of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera Rāṇā [r. 1932-1945] ( Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 39). A certain Jayarāja Śreṣṭha renovated the hiti in 1999 CE (VS 2056) and in 2011 CE (VS 2068) local residents, with the financial support from the Lalitpur Sub-metropolitan City, built a water storage and distribution system for the benefit of the local community. This system is still functioning. A minor renovation of the hiti took place in 2017 CE (VS 2074) when the hitis and phalcās in the Ālko quarter were repaired with funds from the World Bank and the Lalitpur Municipality. Unfortunately, little attention was paid to the use of authentic materials for the renovation. Due to rapid urbanization resulting in groundwater depletion, the flow of water in the hiti considerably decreases during the dry season. The local community cleans and worships the hiti on the day of the Sithinakhaḥ, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.

label: Hona Bāhāḥ (ca. 1895 CE)
description: Hona Bāhāḥ, also known as Hoḍola Vihārā or Kṛṣṇavīra Vihāra, is a one-storey god house located southeast of the Cyasal Square. This independent bāhāḥ was established by Kṛṣṇavīra Prajāpati (Tuisiṃ Āḥju) and is sometimes also referred to as a nani . The front facade resembles a three-bayed phalcā and the sanctum is located behind the central bay. The main statues in the sanctum are Akṣobhya, Tārā and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara. The original Akṣobhya was stolen and replaced with a new one. The northern wall of the sanctum is furnished with latticed woodwork. Above the carved entrance door is a wooden toraṇa with Akṣobhya at the centre, Prajñāpāramitā to the left and Lokeśvara to the right. Statues of Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla are attached to the front facade and a statue of Mañjuvajra resides in a niche on the west interior wall. The roof is covered with traditional tiles. Hona Bāhāḥ is nestled between residential buildings on the west and east, two doors lead to a small courtyard to its south and the main facade faces an rectangular courtyard with a row of residential buildings. A small pañcāvali caitya was established in front of the main sanctum in 1895 CE (NS 1015). There are no records when the bāhāḥ was built, however, it is likely that it was established at the same time as the caitya . Hona Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with different bricks and types of mortar: the sanctum was rebuilt in dacīapā using cement mortar while the other walls consist of māapā , dacīapā and desiapā in mud mortar.

label: Kuladeva Bāhāḥ (built in 1928 CE)
description: Kuladeva Bāhāḥ is a branch of Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). Unlike many other bāhāḥs or their branches, this Bāhāḥ has no proper kvāḥpāḥchẽ (house for the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ‘primary deity’). Instead, a small temple ( kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ ) made of bricks and plastered in cement, houses a brass statue of Akṣobhya as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpādyaḥ inside its sanctum . The temple has a caitya shaped pinnacle, and its main entrance to the sanctum is protected with iron bars. It is capped by a toraṇa and is flanked by a Gaṇeśa (left) and a Mahākāla (right) statue. The current brass made Akṣobhya statue is enshrined recently [1] after the previous one made of stone was stolen from the sanctum in 2012 CE (VS 2069). Two brothers, Kuladeva and Caityarāja (supported by Kuladeva’s son Mānadeva), had jointly built this Bāhāḥ, installed the aforementioned stone statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum, and established a Dharmadhātu Manḍala in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard in 1928 CE (NS 1048). The Caitya, which has also been erected in the courtyard, is probably older than the Bāhāḥ itself. The bell offered to the Caitya in 1920 CE (NS 1040) by the same two brothers has evidential value for dating. Until recently, the sons of Kuladeva and Caityarāja used to perform the daily rituals in this Bāhāḥ. They have also stopped performing its anniversary rituals which used to take place on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha (the Akṣayatṛtīyā day).

label: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (1958 CE)
description: This Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya is located at the south-west corner of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ). Shields above the Caitya's harmikā symbolise the four Tathāgatas: the jewel, lotus, viśvavajra and vajra . Below the dome, one can find statues of the four Tathāgatas: Vairocana (east), Mañjuśrī (north), Vajrasattva (west) and Amitābha (south). In addition to this, four Tārās have been placed at the corners above three layers of lotus petals. The composite of dome and drum contains eight niches and rests in turn on the pericarp of a fully opened lotus flower with three circles of petals. The Four Buddhas have been placed on a throne atop some upward-opening single-layered lotus blossoms. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi have been placed on the eastern, southern, western and northern sides of the Caitya respectively. Akṣobhya’s seat is decorated with images of two elephants and Maitreya. Similarly, the southern side is decorated with images of two horses and Vajrapāṇi, the western side displays peacocks and Padmapāṇi, and the northern side exhibits images of Garuḍas and Mañjuśrī. The lower lotus is decorated with a circle of water motifs and rests upon still another socle. This socle takes a vimśatikoṇa shape and is decorated with vajra symbols. Below this, one can see a lion throne with four sculpted images lions at each of its four corners, as well as images of Caturmahārājas at each of the cardinal directions. Below the throne, one can see a vedikā and a plinth. This Caitya was commissioned by Harṣamuni Śākya in 1958. The anniversary ritual worship of the Caitya is performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.

label: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (1983 CE)
description: The Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Mandira. Generally, caityas follow the pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, this Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya displays statues of Vairocana to the east, Mañjuśrī to the north, Vajrasattva to the west and Amitābha to the south. This monument was constructed in 1983, and its anniversary worship is performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha. Tradition dictates that an umbrella be placed on top of the caitya on the full moon day of Āśvina.

label: Kularatna Vihāra (ca. 1880 CE)
description: Kularatna Vihāra is a branch of Cikã Bahī. It can be accessed via a narrow alley that runs under a residential building on the way to Cyāsal from Bhelāchẽ. The west-facing god house has a carved door, but lacks a toraṇa. There are no stone lions in front of the door and even the panels of the door are not fixed in place. A stone image of Akṣobhya can be found inside the sanctum - this small image is a replacement of the previous one, which was stolen in the 1960s. To the left of Akṣobhya, one can see a stone statue of a six-armed Mañjuvajra. He holds a sword and an arrow in his two right hands and performs varada with the third one. His three left hands can be seen holding a book of the Prajñāpāramitā, a lotus flower and a bow. Tārā sits to the right of Akṣobhya, and is performing varada and abhaya and holding lotus stalks in her two hands. To the left of Tārā, one can find a terracotta image of Red Matsyendranātha. His body is covered with a red cloth. According to local informants, this particular image was installed around 40 years ago. This vihāra is attached to the eastern boundary wall of a courtyard that measures 23 m x 8 m. The courtyard can be accessed through an opening on its western wall, which also contains images of Bhīmasena and Gaṇeśa. The building is a simple one-storey structure, and its back wall shares the courtyard's boundary wall. The three other sides are partitioned with timber lattice work. The main door is to the west, and is a swing door with metal vertical rails. The building is raised above the level of the courtyard in that it sits on a stone plinth of 1.8 m x 2.4 m. It appears that the plinth was recently covered with a concrete flat slab that is supported by brick piers on the western side. The roof has a stūpa finial that has been built with bricks on cement mortar. In front of the sanctum, one can find a small dharmadhātu maṇḍala . The western residential building in front of the vihāra has some remaining traditional wall paintings on the first floor level, though these are rapidly deteriorating. No inscription could be found to provide information about the establishment of this vihāra . However, Gellner (1987, 405) mentions that the nearby Bhaiṣajya Vihāra was established by Jīvanṛsiṃha in 1878 (NS 998). He claims that his eldest son established this Kularatna Vihāra some years later.

label: Ko Bāhāḥ
description: The area around the Kumbheśhvara temple, north of Patan is called Kobāhaḥ. There are numerous references to Ko Bāhāḥ or Ko Vihāra situated in this area dating back to the fourteen century ( Locke 1985, 128). Dozens of late-Malla period inscriptions also use the word Kobāhā to describe the area. These references assert that there was a big monastery called Ko Bāhāḥ in this area. However, Locke (ibid.) doubts that this small Bāhāḥ is identical with the historical Ko Bāhāḥ and assumes that this Bāhāḥ was a branch of Kvā Bāhāḥ. At present, the Bāhāḥ, also called Ituṅ Bāhāḥ, is very small and looks like a śākhāvihāra (branch monastery). It is possible that the Ituṅ Bāhāḥ located in the Ko Bāhāḥ area, was later associated with the name. A pair of stone lions sitting on the sides of the entrance guard the Bāhāḥ. The Carved wooden door is surmounted by a toraṇa with the images of Triratna. First-floor façade has a three-bayed window. Inside the sanctum sanctorum lies a metal statue of Akṣobhya. There was a statue of Cakrasamvara on the first floor, however it is lost. Now only two small statues of Kumārī and Bhairava are lying there. Besides, there is a small wooden caitya . A vajradhātu caitya stands in the courtyard. Locke (ibid.) and Pruscha (1975, 168) mention that there are two stone caityas in the Bāhāḥ complex, but these are not found. No historical record is available to date the Bāhāḥ. Four families associated with the Guji Bāhāḥ Saṅgha were performing the daily and other worships in the Bāhāḥ who around 100 years before got the authority. Since 2000 CE, they have also left the area and their duty. They handed over the authority to a Śākya family living in a house attached to the Bāhāḥ complex. At present, the family is taking care of the Bāhāḥ and performing the worships. Earlier, the annual worship of this Baha was performed in the month of Karttika, but the tradition discontinued about 25 years ago.

label: Sum Bāhāḥ (before 1536 CE)
description: Sum Bāhāḥ is a branch of Jyo Bāhāḥ ( LAL1770 ). It has a two-storied shrine ( dyaḥchẽ ) which faces west. The roof of the dyaḥchẽ which is supported by the plain struts was originally tiled with the jhĩgaṭīs slates, but it is now covered with the corrugated pewter sheets. [1] The first floor has a trikhā -window flanked by tiki -windows. Also, a sacred place for Bāhāḥ’s esoteric deity ( āgama ) is on the second floor. The sanctum ( garbhagṛha ) of the dyaḥchẽ is on its first floor. Previously, a wooden toraṇa on which the images of Akṣobhya (in the middle), and Prañāpāramitā and Lokeśvara (to the right and left of Akṣobhya) was kept above the main door to the dyaḥchẽ (cf. Locke 1985, 77). However, this disappeared or most probably got stolen sometime before 1985 CE. A stone statue of Akṣobhya, flanked by the Sūrya (the god Sun) statue, has been enshrined in the sanctum sanctorum as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ . [2] A Dharmadhātujinālaṃkṛta Caitya and Dharmadhātu Maṇdala (erected in NS 984, i.e. 1864 CE and NS 1057, i.e. 1937 CE, respectively) are established in the Bāhā’s courtyard. [3] Although no documented evidence is so far found to date the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction, a copy of the document reporting the various events suggests that it must have been built before 1536 CE. [4] When King Raṇa Bahādura (r. 1777-1799) confiscated guṭhī land in the Kathmandu Valley, large portion of guṭhī land of this Bāhāḥ, too, was confiscated. [5] Previously, four Śākya families were involved to perform the daily rituals having endowed two ropanīs of land (from each family). However, only the family of Puṇyarāja Śākya (Śukrarāja Śākya) carries out this task now. The Yogāmbara worship which used to take place every year (on the 10 th of the dark fortnight of Māgha) does not take place anymore in the Bāhāḥ. The dyaḥchẽ was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes. The Lalitpur Metropolitan Office has recently allocated 5 lakhs to renovate it. Footnotes ^ This dyaḥchẽ has no pinnacle above its roof. ^ The Akṣobhya statue is dressed in lhegā . ^ Previously, a caitya with a gilded Buddha ( suvarṇa Buddha) statue was erected in the place where the Dharmadhātujinālaṃkṛta Caitya has been erected now. At present, no one knows whereabouts of this caitya . It is believed that this Bāhāḥ was named Suvarṇapura Mahāvirā because of this gilded Buddha statue. ^ This document mentions a dispute from NS 656 (1536 CE) between the members of Sum Bāhāḥ and their neighbor Phyāku Mulmī. ^ Twenty ropanīs of land belonging to the Bāhāḥ was returned to the Bāhāḥ’s guṭhī in 1862.

label: Caitya (1944 CE)
description: This Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and exhibits a hybrid design. The bottom half features elements typical of a j vālāvali caitya such as lions at the corners of its base and a lotus pedastal, while the upper half resembles a ś ikharakūṭa caitya with its Lokeśvara statues and four Buddhas attached to the dome. The Caitya is in a good condition and has been cleaned recently. The inscription of the Caitya mentions that its construction was funded by Nararāja Pāneju in 1944 CE. Nararāja also established a guṭhī to perform the daily and anniversary ritual worship of the Caitya. However, his descendants sold their property and moved away from the locality, selling the guṭhī land and thus bringing an end to the daily worship. The Caitya's anniversary worship is performed on the full moon day of Āśvina.

label: Mūchẽ Āgama (ca. early 15th cent. CE)
description: Mūchẽ Āgama is located to the north of the Bahādur Śāha. The building can be accessed through a small door opening on the western boundary wall. The Āgama was located at the south of a small courtyard facing north. The main entry door on the ground floor can be reached by climbing up on to a raised plinth guarded by two small stone lions. The main carved door is flanked by two small blind windows on either sides. A small secondary entry door on the principal façade (the eastern end of the building) leads to a stairway. There were two three-fold pasukā jhyāḥ on the first and second floor, both of which were salvaged after the earthquake. The historical name of the Āgama is Maṇichẽ, meaning a house located in the Maṇigala Ṭola. The word maṇichẽ has changed into mūchẽ over the course of time. This building appears to be a normal residential building, however, this is in fact the āgãchẽ of the Jośīs of Bakhumbāhāla and Kisis (Śreṣṭha) of Ombāhāla. The Rājopādhyāyas of the Svãtha Ṭola perform the daily ritual worship here. Manamāneśvarī, the lineage deity of Licchavi kings who was worshipped before Taleju was brought to the Valley, is also worshipped inside this shrine. The Āgama used to house a collection of the swords of kings. When a ruling king died, his sword was preserved here. Jośī (2065, 16-17) states that there were once more than 30 swords inside this Āgama. The three-storey building of the Āgama was heavily damaged in the 2015 earthquake and now only the front wall of the ground floor remains. The main deity has been relocated to a neighboring house and various small images have been preserved in the Patan Museum. No historical record confirming the initial construction of the shrine is available. A Gaṇeśa statue located to the north-west was established in 1434 (NS 558). This provides grounds to assume that the Āgama may also have been constructed around this time, or may even pre-date the statue.

label: Bhagavān Degaḥ
description: Bhagavān Degaḥ is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ). It was originally built as a two-tiered temple and later converted into a hybrid structure with a domed roof. Bhagavān Degaḥ is partly depicted in a watercolour by Henry Ambrose Oldfield , dated 1857. This painting serves as the sole documentation of the temple’s restorations and reconfigurations over the past 150 years. No records of its initial construction could be found. It can be assumed that the temple was severely damaged in the 1934 earthquake and was later rebuilt in its current shape. The lower roof was preserved but the upper roof was replaced by a plastered brick dome with a gilt copper finial. Later, the lower roof was rebuilt with a brass sheet cover and decorative eaves. The original open pillar arcade was closed off with lattice woodwork and a door was installed in the east façade. This work was probably carried out some time between 1980-1990. The inner cella was partly covered with industrial tiles and a new door and a steel scissor gate have also been installed for security purposes. Today, only a few of the original components survive; these include the carved pillars, corbels and cross beams. Most of the edge stones and original tile floors have been lost.
