Until a few decades ago this temple was known as the Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara Temple. Even the 2002 book Cultural Heritage of Bungmati (in p. 53) refers to it as the temple of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara. A statue of Śākyamuni Buddha was enshrined in this temple around four decades ago. Before this, the sanctum of the temple was empty. The temple's new name of Bhagavān Degaḥ is closely related to this new deity. Elderly people in Bungmati tell of a legend which links this temple with the Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara Temple of Nālā (in the Kabhrepalnacok district). According to this story, the idol of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara (which is currently in Nālā) was originally to be found in this temple. Some time ago, the idol disappeared from the temple of Bungmati. Eventually, it was found lying in the mud somewhere. ‘ Nāla ’ is a Newari word meaning mud. The deity found in the ‘ nāla’ was then established in its current location. Only the Pāneju Saṅgha of Bungmati have the right to perform the life-cycle (daśakarma ) rites of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara in Nālā. A group of eight p ānejus from Bungmati goes to Nālā for this purpose every year on the full moon day of Phāguna. Like the temple of Nālā, this temple also faces east. Since the Buddha statue was established in the temple, two families of Śākyas and Tulādhara have taken on responsibility for performing the ritual worships. A procession now also takes place in Bungmati on the day of Buddha Jayantī (the full moon day of Vaiśākha). On this day, people place the deity on a cot and carry him around the surrounding area of Bungmati.

label: Gaṇeśa Mandira
description: Gaṇeśa Mandira is located in Kotā Ṭola, Bungmati. The Tulādhara and Mālī caste groups worship this Gaṇeśa as their local deity. The mandira faces south and has a jhĩgaṭī tiled roof supported by carved struts. A metal pinnacle and parasol can be found atop the roof. A toraṇa has been placed above the carved wooden door. The main façade is decorated with latticed woodwork and two small latticed windows have been installed in the eastern and western walls of the temple. An aniconic stone image of Gaṇeśa with a metal crown on his head is enshrined in the sanctum. Besides the main shrine, many iconic and aniconic stone images can be seen around the sanctum. A wooden toraṇa is attached to the eastern wall. There was a hiti (stepwell) to the east of the temple until a few decades ago. However, it gradually turned into a rubbish dumping site and was eventually covered up with mud. Before the hiti was completely filled in, some of the statues were removed and relocated to this temple and the nearby Licchavi caitya (BUN0026) . The temple was reconstructed in 2003. The projecting roof on the northern side was left unfinished during the reconstruction process, meaning that the temple's structure appears unbalanced. Local residents traditionally come to this temple to worship Gaṇeśa before they begin any other auspicious rituals such as initiation ceremonies, marriage or jaṃko (Skt. bhīmarathārohaṇa ) . The Kusle (Kapālī) community were responsible for taking care of this temple until a few years ago. However, now that this community no longer takes care of this temple there are no official caretakers ( dyaḥpāḥlāḥs ).

label: Iku Bāhāḥ (before 1878 CE)
description: Iku Bāhāḥ is one of the branches of Bu Bāhāḥ ( LAL0440 ) and is located to the north-west of the main bāhāḥ . For this reason, this monastic building is also called ikuli or yakuli , meaning ‘north-west direction’. Nowadays, a family living in Mūladuvāḥ Kavaḥ (Nānicāyāḥ Kavaḥ) of Bu Bāhāḥ takes care of this branch. Residential buildings surround the three-storey monastic building. The main entrance is flanked by a lion to the right and a śārdūla (leopard) to the left. Both of these statues were established in 1885 CE. The entrance to the sanctum is clad in brass and is surmounted by a copper repoussé toraṇa showing Akṣobhya in the middle with Prajñāpāramitā on his right and Lokeśvara on his left. An image of Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva has also been placed on the upper part of the toraṇa. The door to the shrine is flanked by small latticed windows, with a stone statue of Hanumān attached to the wall above the left window and an image of Gaṇeśa kept above the right window. On the left wall one can also find a stone statue of Mahākāla with three heads and four arms holding khaḍga , kartṛ , khaṭvāṅga and kapāla . The main deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ) is Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva. The façade of the first storey contains a latticed window flanked by two inscriptions and two smaller latticed windows, whilst the second storey has a large plain window. Historical photos of the bāhāḥ show that it once had a jhĩgaṭī -tiled roof. However, the building is currently under reconstruction. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala and a śikharakūṭa caitya have been erected in the courtyard. In the 2015 earthquakes, a building standing to the right of the bāhāḥ collapsed and fell down, destroying two storeys of the bāhāḥ . This building was completely removed after the earthquake and is now under construction. The Lalitpur Municipality has provided 2.5 million rupees for its reconstruction. A photograph of the bāhāḥ complex taken circa 1974 (published in Pruscha 1975 C/P-47) shows that the ground floor of the bāhāḥ (as previously reconstructed) is similar to its current structure, with the exception that dāci apā (bricks) were used instead of mā apā (bricks) and the white plastered cornice was replaced with decorative bricks. The height of the first floor has been increased considerably (by approx. 50 cm) and the three old latticed windows were replaced with new ones of different sizes and proportions. A new carved brick cornice was added above them, matching the design of the ground floor cornice. The second floor now features a new wall made using dāci apā and a new window frame.

label: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (1964 CE)
description: The Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala, all of which are alligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira. Generally, caityas follow a pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, within this Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya Vairocana is located to the east, Mañjuśrī to the north, Vajrasattva to the west and Amitābha to the south.

label: Gaṇeśa Phalcā 2
description: Gaṇeśa Phalcā 2 is located to the south of Gaṇeśa Mandira ( SUN0102 ) and to the east of Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira ( SUN0100 ). This one-storey RCC Phalcā is adjacent to the eastern entrance of the Bhṛṅgāreśvara temple complex. Before it was dismantled around 1986, the Phalcā had a gable roof with tiles. This roof was then replaced by a concrete slab supported by three RCC columns during its reconstruction. The rear brick masonry wall made from mud mortar and stones on the plinth are the only traces of the original structure that remain. Dāphā Bhajana is performed inside the Phalcā, and so it is also known as Dāphā Phalcā. The monument finds most use during festivals.

label: Devarāja Bāhāḥ (1902 CE)
description: Devarāja Bāhāḥ is located in Pyagaḥ Thā̃ to the east of the street that runs from Gāḥ Bāhāḥ ( LAL0510 ) to Pim Bāhāḥ Caitya ( LAL0750 ). A somewhat hidden narrow door leads to the bāhāḥ’s courtyard, where a small shrine of Akṣobhya is attached to a six-storey building. The shrine has a small door surmounted by a toraṇa showing an image of Akṣobhya and flanked by latticed windows on either side. The structure has a two-tiered lime plaster roof with a towering bell-shaped pinnacle and a small stone caitya . Carved struts support the roof. In the courtyard, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya (140 cm high). Paved with brick tiles, the sunken courtyard measures 235 cm × 275 cm. A stone inscription attached to the left wall of the shrine mentions the date of its initial construction. A member of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440) called Devarāja Vajrācārya built this bāhāḥ in 1902, one year after he constructed the dharmadhātujinālaya caitya in the courtyard. It was worshipped daily and was a site for other religious activities to take place until the grandson of the founder, Dharmarāja Vajrācārya, passed away. The courtyard has since fallen into disuse and has become a dumping site for rubbish.

label: Yaṅgaḥ Bāhāḥ (built before 1039 CE)
description: Yaṅga Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). This Bāhāḥ faces east, and its roof is tiled with jhĩgaṭī . While the shrine for the esoteric deity ( āgaṃ ) is located on the first floor, the sanctum ( garbhagṛha ) is on the ground floor. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is the bāhāḥ’s primary deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ). This stone statue lost its authenticity, since it has been painted in enamel paint. A Śikharakūṭa Caitya in the couirtyuard which was renovated in NS 1063 (1943 CE). The bāhāḥ is mentioned in a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 159 (1039 CE). ( Kölver & Śākya 1985, 103). The Bāhāḥ had been abandoned for a long time, and consequently turned into ruins. The local elders mentioned that it was haunted even during the daytime. Since it was not possible to run the daily operations of the Bāhāḥ, its saṅgha members, Yogaratna Śākya, Munirāja Śākya, Teja Bahādura Śākya, and others, handed over the Bāhāḥ to a Bhikṣu Saṅgha (an organization of some monks who practice at the Therāvāda school of Buddhism) in VS 2000 (1943 CE). Later in VS 2007 (1950 CE), it came under the jurisdiction of this organization ( Śākya 2053, 3). Following the hand over of the bāhāḥ, it was named after a Sri Lankan monk, Sumaṅgala Vihāra by Nārada Mahāsthavīra ( Śākya 2053, 1). No one addresses henceforth the Bāhāḥ by its old name. Contemporary buildings surround the Bāhāḥ in the present-day, and it serves as a learning centre for the Therāvāda Buddhism.

label: Bare Nani (17th cent.)
description: Bare Nani is located to the south-east of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) in Bungmati. This nani is also referred to as a bāhāḥ ( Locke 1985, 239) even though its architectural design does not much resemble this kind of structure . A pair of stone lions have been placed at its entrance, however the building lacks an āgãchẽ (a shrine of the esoteric clan deity) which is normally the main feature of a bāhāḥ . However, there is an āgãchẽ in one of the houses located at the south-eastern corner of the courtyard. Bare Nani is primarily related to the Śākyas who are priests in the Hayagrīva Mandira ( BUN0002 ) living nearby. The saṅgha of the Śākyas is also active; for example, the initiation rituals of local Śākya boys are performed in this nani . A vajradhātu caitya stands in the middle of the courtyard, and statues of the Four Buddhas have been placed around it with one at each of the four cardinal directions. The caitya has been covered with a thick lime paint that covers the motifs on the harmikā and trayodaśa-bhuvana . In front of the caitya, one can find a dharmadhātu maṇḍala and an Akṣobhya shrine, both of which were established in 1980. Local residents claim that this caitya was established before the Red (Rāto) Matsyendranātha was brought to the Kathmandu Valley. However, there is no evidence to support this claim. The caitya was repaired in 1659, and the courtyard was paved with bricks in 1682. This year also saw two lion statues placed at the entrance of the courtyard. A parasol is offered to the caitya every year on the full moon days of Āśvina and Caitra. A feast is also organised on these dates.

label: Dabū and temporary shrine
description: There are many dab ūs (traditional platforms) in the old settlements of Kathmandu Valley. Most of them were made in the Malla period and were used for the performances of dramas and dances. An inscription found in Nārāyaṇacaura, Naksal from the reign of King Jayadeva the second (713-733 CE) mentions two platforms known as ponḍimaṇḍapikā and prekṣaṇamaṇḍapikā (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, 569 and K. Tamo t 2013, 20). In the Malla period, many dances and dramas were performed in dabūs, especially during festivals and ceremonies ( K. Tamo t 2013, 20). Buṅgamatī's Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) collapsed in the devastating earthquakes of 2015. Fortunately, at that time the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ normally enshrined there was on a chariot travelling from Buṅgadyaḥ towards Patan and so remained unharmed. Since the restoration of the temple is likely to last many years, a temporary shrine building has been built on the foundation of this dabū to house the deity. This shrine building measures 412 × 412 cm and was built using regular brick in mud mortar. It is covered by a roof made of steel trusses, plywood and metal sheets. There were two large stone lions guarding the northern entrance and two smaller lions in front of the southern entrance of the Karuṇāmaya Temple. These have been moved to stand in front of the dabū . A bell suspended from a stone frame was also moved from its original location to the left of the shrine’s entrance. Following the 2015 collapse of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) this temporary shrine was built to house the main deity of Buṅgadyaḥ (BUN0001-008). Also, two large stone lions (BUN0001-008), two small stone lions (BUN0001-009), and a bell suspended from a stone stand (BUN0001-010) were moved from the temple to the front of this temporary shrine. No sources can be found with which to date the initial construction of this dabū . Every 12 years, two dances are performed here: jalapyākhã (a dance from Harisiddhi) and gathupyākhã (a dance from Thecho).

label: Yaṃgubāhāḥ Sataḥ
Phalcā 4113
Degutale Mandira
Kṛṣṇa Mandira
Cī Bāhāḥ Nani (ca. 17th cent. CE)
description: Cī Bāhāḥ Nani is located to the east of the street that runs from Cyāsala to Olakhu. It is known as Ci Bāhāḥ Libi (a courtyard with a caitya ) amongt the local residents. The main facade of the structure has two columns that support a door screen between them. The door has a toraṇa above it and a metal screen to protect the image housed inside the sanctum. The roof has a plastered coping on the boundary wall and a small pinnacle. A cornice band runs along the boundary wall. Although Nanis are often associated with their main Bāhāḥs, this Nani has no association with any other major Bāhāḥ. It solely belongs to the Prajāpati family. Locke (1985, 72) assumes that Nani's present shrine was constructed after the 1934 earthquake. The shrine lacks many major features that are typical to a bāhāḥ . The main shrine is attached to a boundary wall on the south. The sanctum holds a north-facing stone statue of Akṣobhya wearing a lhegā (metal attire). Following the theft of the original statue a few years ago, this new statue is now protected by a metal grill. Broken pieces of glass have been embedded in the boundary wall for further protection. Above the door, one can find a toraṇa with a lotus petal in its centre. A stone relief depicting the Five Buddhas is placed underneath the image of Akṣobhya. The inscription on the pedestal of these images is now illegible. Images of Nārāyaṇa, Vajradhara, Mañjuśrī, Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla have been placed in a line on the wall. Outside, a Śikharakūṭa Caitya sits in front of the main shrine. The courtyard is paved with concrete tiles. The earliest inscription mentioning this Nani is dated to NS 796.

label: Taḥdhãlibi Bāhāḥ (1598 CE)
description: Taḥdhãlibi Bāhāḥ can be accessed via a narrow alleyway that runs underneath a residential house, to the north of the way from Uku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ) to Ubāhā Bahī ( LAL2280 ). The main shrine of the bāhāḥ is a plastered structure that is raised above the ground on a plinth. The roof of the temple has a stūpa as its finial, and the temple structure itself is decorated with pilasters at each corner. The main sanctum faces west, and its entrance is emphasised by the triangular motif that sits above it. A small dharmadhātu maṇḍala (45 cm high) and a vajradhātu caitya (145 cm high) that sits on a square base of 120 cm are both lined up centrally to the west of the main shrine. This ensemble of monuments can be found towards the south-eastern corner of the courtyard. The courtyard measures 11.7 m × 9.2 m and is paved in telia tiles. A narrow alley to the north-western corner leads on to the Dune Bāhāḥ ( LAL2300 ). Generally, this place is not referred to as a bāhāḥ ; instead, local residents call it a libi/coka (courtyard). Locke (1985) also does not include this monument in his list of vihāras . However, Śākya (1994, 117-18) counts it as a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260 ). The structure of this vihāra differs from that of other vihāras . A cement-plastered shrine topped with a stūpa -shaped pinnacle stands on the eastern side of the courtyard. There are no traditional carvings nor decorative objects in this shrine. Nāmasaṅgīti is enshrined in the sanctum as the main deity, and images of Mahākāla and Gaṇeśa have been attached respectively to the northern and the southern walls of the shrine. The shrine can be circumambulated via a narrow passage. A largely effaced stone inscription stands at the southeast corner of the caitya . Śākya (1994, 117-18) has identified the date of the inscription as NS 718. However, the inscription is now mostly illegible and so the date could not be confirmed.

label: Ikhālakhu Bāhāḥ
description: This small courtyard, known as Ikhālakhu Bāhāḥ, is located to the east of Ikhālakhu coka . The courtyard is behind a row of residential buildings near the Ikhālakhu Jahru . It is paved with stone flooring. This small courtyard is located to the east of Ikhālakhu and can be reached through a narrow alley. Measuring 6.5m x 3.75m, it consists of a raised plinth on the northern wall containing three small statues with stone roofs, atop of which are small stupas. At the center is a śikharakūṭa caitya with a base measuring 140 x 140 cm and a height of 170 cm. A d harmadhātu maṇḍala (90 cm tall) adjoins it on its northern side. A small caitya (70cm tall) can be found on the southern plinth attached to the building, and appears to be in a neglected state. A bell hangs on two stone pillars (13 x 13 cm and 170 cm high) to the east of the courtyard. This tiny courtyard reaches the minimum requirements for a Bāhāḥ as defined by Locke. Bruce Owens notes that the kwāḥpāḥ dyaḥ , caitya , and other features are under threat as this space has been used to store lumber (and now detritus from the reconstruction) since at least 2008. Indeed, most of the features generally found in a vihāra cannot be found here. There is, for instance, no god-house ( dyaḥchẽ ). Local people therefore consider this place to just be a coka rather than a vihāra . Three south-facing and connected shrines house the main deities of the vihāra. When Locke (1985, 140) studied this place, there was an image of Akṣobhya inside the middle shrine, an image of Prajñāpāramitā inside the shrine right to it and an image of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara inside the left shrine, however these images have since been stolen. In their place, statues of a doner in the act of praying have been installed inside the middle shrine, whilst the right-hand shirine now contains an image of Lakṣmī holding a lotus flower in her hand. The left-hand shrine has been furnished with an image of a two-handed Lokeśvara holding a lotus in his left hand and with his right hand in a varada gesture. Above the middle and the left shrine, one can find images of Mahākāla and three doners. These have been placed in a disorganized way. Local people claim that this Bāhāḥwas made by Śreṣṭhas. Apart from this, nothing more is known about its history. Inside the courtyard, there is one śikharakūṭa caitya and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala . At the eastern corner of the courtyard is a bell that was donated in NS 1049, and at the southern corner one can find another small caitya . Note that the illustration identified by Locke (1985, 141I) as Ikhalakhu Baha is actually Iku Baha, and the photograph of Ikhalaku (mis-labeled as Iku Baha) is actually on p. 139.

label: Vãlā Bāhāḥ (1921 CE)
description: Vãlā Bāhāḥ, a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ ( LAL0440) , is located to the east of Pūrṇacandī Temple and to the north of the street that leads to Ikhālakhu. The bāhāḥ can be accessed by turning left down a narrow alleyway. It is called a bāhāḥ or vihāra even though it lacks a kvāḥpāḥchẽ . A small shrine of the bāhāḥ is attached to the southern wall of the courtyard. The wooden carved door of the sanctum is surmounted by a toraṇa displaying an image of Vajrasattva. However, Locke (1985, 169) identifies the deity as Akṣobhya. Inside the sanctum, one can find a north-facing stone image of Akṣobhya. There are two small niches on either side of the shrine. According to Vajrācārya (1993, 134) there was once an image of Mahākāla in the western niche. However, this is now missing. The main temple structure is built on a double plinth. A stone threshold on the upper plinth provides the base for the carved wooden structure, which is open at three sides and has a rear boundary wall for support. The structure has two tiers of cement roof and a bell-shaped stūpa as its finial. Ten struts support the roof. There is a dharmadhātu jinālaya caitya in front of the main shrine. Hela Thakuṃ built this bāhāḥ in 1921 (NS 1041) in memory of her late son Harṣavīra Vajrācārya. He was the eldest son of Dhīrjavīra Kampanī, a famous devotee and donor living in Dhyākva Nhūchẽ Kavaḥ of Bu Bāhāḥ. A ceremony called vãlā was organised on the inauguration day of the bāhāḥ , during which a procession passed through the main bāhās and bahīs of Patan. This bāhāḥ is named after the procession ( Vajrācārya 1933, 134).

label: Chāya Bāhāḥcā (1659 CE)
description: Three branches of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ are located in Chāḥ Bāhāḥ ṭola . All of these branches are known as Chāḥ Bāhāḥ and so it is unclear which one is actually the Chāḥ Bāhāḥ. This Bāhāḥ is also called Bāhāḥcā in reference to its small size. It is located ca. 65 meters east of the Chāya Bāhāḥ Hiti. The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ can be reached by passing through a narrow alley and a carved door. The small courtyard measures 620 cm x 445 cm and houses an octagonal aṣṭakoṇaparivṛtākāra caitya . The main entrance to the Bāhāḥ is through a carved door, though there is also a plain door and a lattice window on its ground floor. Six statues flank the main door, with Khyāka, Gaṇeśa and Sāriputra to the left and Kavã, Mahākāla and Maudgalyāyana to the right. The statues of Khāka and Kavã are an interesting addition to this Buddhist monastic building, as they are more commonly found in the Śākta temples of the Valley. A pair of three praying wheels are fixed above the statues, and a wooden toraṇa with the images of Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara is fixed above the door. The Bāhāḥcā has a cement-plastered façade and a pāsukhā jhyāḥ on its first floor. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in its sanctum and an aniconic stone attached to the left wall of the building is worshipped as Bhairava. Relying on an inscription, Locke (1985, 44) dates the Bāhāḥ to NS 779 (1659 CE). A completely effaced stone inscription is attached to the wall of the building and is likely the one that Locke used for this. Four families take care of the Bāhāḥ, performing its daily ritual worships and other social-religious activities.

label: Cilancva Bāhāḥ (ca. 1515 CE)
description: The Cilancva area is the highest point in Kirtipur, located in its eastern part. A huge Cilancva Caitya ( KIR0001 ) stands at the centre of the site. There are numerous other Buddhist monuments in the Caitya premises, which is collectively known as Cilancva Bāhāḥ, a major Buddhist monastery in Kirtipur. It is also called Jagatapāla Mahāvihāra, Mū Bāhāḥ, Gũ Vihāra, Padmakāṣṭhagīri Vihāra, and Kipū Bāhāḥ etc. Kirtipur was under the Patan rule during the medieval period. Thus, Cilancva Bāhāḥ is listed as one of the Mahāvihāras of Patan. The Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī (19.3.26) also mentions that King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla listed this Bāhāḥ as one of the fifteen Mahāvihāras maintained by Patan. The members of this Bāhāḥ still part take in the Buddhist rituals and festivals held in Patan such as the Samyak Festival and other seasonal processions. Majority of the scholars conclude that this Bāhāḥ was constructed by Jagata Varmā, a Mahāpātra of Patan, almost at the same time when he constructed Cilancva Caitya ( KIR0001 ) in 1515 CE. However, the inscription recording the construction of this Caitya does not explicitly mention Cilancva Bāhāḥ, but refers to this area as 'Padmakāṣṭhagīri which resembles the heaven ( padmakāṣṭhagīri bhanne nāmale svargajastai suhāiraheko ṭhāũ ). It indicates that Jagata Pāla could have established a Bāhāḥ called Padmakāṣṭhagīri in the Cilancva premises which was later known as Cilancva Bāhāḥ. [1] He also renovated Bāghabhairava Mandira ( KIR0004 ) in 1571 CE (NS 635). Since his wife Rūpalakṣmī (cf. D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, 478) was from Kirtipur ( Locke 1985, 180), she could have encouraged him to construct and renovate these highly significant monuments. The southern entrance to Cilancva Caitya and the main entrance to Cilancva Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ are parallel to each other, revealing the architectural similarity of both monuments. A pair of lions installed in 1716 CE (NS 836) flanks the dyaḥchẽ ’s main entrance. Similarly, two metal statues (Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana) are placed to the right and to the left of the entrance respectively, which is a common feature of the bāhāḥs . A carved wooden toraṇa also crowns the entrance. Right above the toraṇa , a pasukājhyāḥ can be seen on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor. In addition to the main entrance, the dyaḥchẽ has two additional doors in its façade. Two trikhājhyāḥs are also installed on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor, right above these additional doors. The wooden toraṇa above the main entrance was stolen sometime ago, thus the toraṇa , crowning the eastern door, was shifted here. The toraṇas , kept above its eastern door, were removed during the renovation of the dyaḥchẽ building in 2015 CE. A statue of Cakrasamvara is concentrated as the āgaṃdyaḥ on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor. Until a few decades ago, one could see some traditional wall paintings on the first floor. They were completely destroyed during the renovation of the building (cf. Ś . Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 67). The first floor is now empty and used by the members of the saṅgha for organising the community feasts, lectures, seminars etc. There is a balcony on the façade of this floor. The roof of the dyaḥchẽ is tiled with jhĩgaṭī and a pura crowned by three pinnacles is installed on its top. Locke (1985, 180) mentions the beams, which support the aforementioned balcony, bearing the inscriptions from 1629 CE (NS 749) and 1680 CE (NS 800). They suggest that the Bāhāḥ must have been renovated in those dates. A local resident named Candramāna Vajrācārya repaired the roof in around 1889 CE after it was destroyed by a wind ( Ś . Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 68). The latest renovation of the dyaḥchẽ was carried out by the Department of Archaeology after it was destroyed during the 2015 CE earthquakes. Cilancva Bāhāḥ has a saṅgha consisting of the members from the Śākya and Vajrācārya clans. Each Vajrācārya member is responsible to carry out the daily worship for two weeks. The ritual worship is followed by a traditional music, gambāḥsĩ , which is a unique feature of the major bāhāḥs of Patan. The anniversary worship of the Bāhāḥ is held on the full moon day of Asoja. The statue of Cakrasamvara, concerted inside the āgaṃ, is worshiped by the Pradhāna caste community members of Kirtipur on the dark moon day of Vaiśākha (the Mātātīrtha Aũśī day) as their clan deity. The Bāhāḥ had a guṭhī consisting of six ropānīs of land for each elder member ( thakālī ) of the saṅgha for performing the daily and annual rituals. In addition to this, the guṭhī had a pond and flower garden. However, the mentioned guṭhī property cannot be traced out in present-day. The Bāhāḥ had a huge collection of metal statues dating from the seventh and eighth centuries. Because of a dispute that arose amongst the saṅgha members in around 1980 CE, the statues were handed over to the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and National Museum (cf. Ś . Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 68-69). Footnotes ^ This Bāhāḥ is referred to as ‘Padmakāṣṭhagīri Gũ Vihāra concerted according to the customs’ in the invitation letter sent from Paśupati Bāhāḥ to the member of Cilancva Bāhāḥ in 1574 (NS 694) requesting them to participate to the Samyak festival (cf. Vajrācārya VS 2061, 117). Since the invitation letter does not refer to the Bāhāḥ as consecrated by Jagatapāla, one may cast doubt on whether he was its initial constructor.

label: Yākaḥ Bāhāḥ (built in 1647 CE)
description: Yāka Bāhāḥ is located on the northwestern part of the Cilancva Caitya premises ( KIR0001 ) and is one of the branches ( kacā ) of Cilancva Mahāvihāra ( KIR0002) . The Bāhāḥ is also called Jīvadharma Mahāvihāra (see the inscription from NS 801 below), and its courtyard can be entered through an astonishingly carved wooden door. A set of artistically carved trikhā windows can be seen above this door. The Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ (house for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity) is built in the courtyard, facing east. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ (primary deity) inside the sanctum, which is located on the dayaḥchẽ’s ground floor. Besides the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ , there were several other small Buddhist statues and caityas inside the sanctum, however, they were stolen in the course of time. A pair of lions and elephants (established in 1710 CE, i.e., 830 NS) are installed on either side of the entrance to the sanctum. The entrance is adorned with traditional carvings but has no toraṇa above it. The dyaḥchẽ’s first floor has a set of pasukā windows, and its roof is covered with corrugated pewter sheets ( jastāpātā ). The inscription dating 1680 CE (801 NS) installed in the Bāhāḥ premises attests that Yākaḥ Bāhāḥ was constructed in 1647 CE (767 NS) by the Rathasyana Vajrācārya, his son Jīvarāja, and other family members. It also mentions that King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, too, was present during the inaugural ceremony of the Bāhāḥ. Jīvarāja, the main founder of the Bāhāḥ, died sixteen years after its completion. Several statues of Buddha, as well as, Lokeśvara, Prajñāpāramitā, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla statues were installed in the Bāhāḥ premises in the memory of Jivarāja by his family members. On the same date, his two sons also endowed four and a half ropanīs of land and established a guṭhī to sponsor the Bāhāḥ’s anniversary rituals. The other inscriptions (see below) installed in the Bāhāḥ suggest that a number of statues and architectural artifacts were installed here in the late medieval period. In 1970s, the statue of Cakrasamvara and other metal statues enshrined inside the āgaṃ (the shrine on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor built for the Bāhāḥ’s esoteric deities and rituals), were also stolen. Due to the lack of regular maintenance, the roof of the dyaḥchẽ collapsed in 2009 CE, and covered the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ . In 2011CE, some residents of the region restored the roof, covering it with corrugated pewter sheets ( jastāpātā ) funded by the local government. The building which has the main entrance to the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard was damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes. Due to a dispute over its ownership, no one has renovated it since then. Although the inscription (see below) offers a detailed account of the traditions of daily worship, annual rituals, lighting up oil lamp on the full moon day of Kārtika, and so forth to be performed in the Bāhāḥ, no one carries out these rituals in the present-day. Until two decades ago, a Vajrācārya caste member used to perform the daily worship and annual rituals in the Bāhāḥ. Unfortunately, no one took over these tasks after he died. There is no one left who is directly related to this Bāhāḥ, thus it is slowly falling into oblivion.

label: I Bāhāḥ (16th cent. CE)
description: I Bāhāḥ is located approximately 50 metres south of Ikhālakhu Square on the way to Tabāhāl, and lies on the right-hand side of the street. The Bāhāḥ can be accessed through an opening on a boundary wall to the east. It has been heavily reconstructed and was converted to a four-storey residential building after the 2015 earthquakes. The original architecture of the building has been completely destroyed, so that only traces of the brass-clad door, two blind windows and some layers of cornices remain today (in 2019). The main building is raised on a plinth which is 60 cm high. At the centre of the stone-paved courtyard one can find a vajradhātu caitya and a dharmādhātu maṇḍala . The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings on three of the four cardinal directions, with the eastern side as the exception. The courtyard has two alleyways that lead out to the smaller courtyards; these can be found to its west and its south. The Bāhāḥ is a private vihāra constructed by a Joshi family; it is not a branch of any larger bāhāḥ . Images of lions sitting on elephants can be found on either side of the main entrance, and small carved windows adorn the wall here. Upon entering the sanctum, one immediately sees an image of Akṣobhya facing to the east. Two brass statues of Yama holding kāladaṇḍa (the staff of death) and pāśa (a noose) are also housed in the sanctum, with one on either side of the main door. An empty triangular niche to the left of the door is worshipped as Hanumān. Accoding to Pruscha (1975, 133), this vihāra was constructed in the 16th century. According to Locke (1985, 140) two metal flags used to flank the door and a toraṇa was installed above the main entrance. This contained an image of Akṣobhya. However, it seems that the toraṇa was removed by the residing family of the vihāra some time around 2008. Moreover, Locke states that a trikhā jhyāla (triple window) and a bāku jhyāla (lit. halved window) can be found in the façade of the first floor. The building was severely damaged and was no longer safe to live in. Therefore the owner demolished the building and reconstructed it in a modern style. After the reconstruction the family sold the building. Local people say that the family also sold the ground floor of the building where the kvāpādyaḥ of the vihāra is enshrined. The bell was donated in VS 1959.

label: Thapāḥ Bahī
description: Thapāḥ Bahī is a branch of Guji Bāhāḥ and is located at Thapāḥ Ṭola near to Thapāḥ Hiṭī. A series of steps to the north of the Bahī lead up to its courtyard. There is no gate at the courtyard's entrance, which is unusual for this kind of monument . The god house of this Bahī is very simple, and lacks both a toraṇa above the door as well as the stone lions one usually finds in front of such a structure. A historical photo of the Bahī printed in Pruscha (1975, 196) shows that the god house once had a tiled roof with dormer ( bhaipvāḥ ) on top. However, later photos published in Locke (1985, 198) show CGI sheets covering the roof, and indeed this is still the case. The first floor of the god house has a simple lattice window on its façade and an āgamachẽ inside it. The ground floor of the house contains a sanctum with a stone image of an east-facing Akṣobhya. The statue's body is covered with metal cloth ( hẽgā ). A miniature image of this larger one can be found next to it. The god house was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquake and is now supported by wooden columns. A Phalcā containing an image of Mahākāla sits on the northern side of the courtyard. Meanwhile, an Aśoka Caitya marks the centre of the courtyard.

label: Vasu Bāhāḥ (built around 1938 CE)
description: Vasu Bāhāḥ is a branch of Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). Unlike other bāhāḥs in Patan and elsewhere, this Bāhāḥ does not have a proper shrine ( kvāḥpāḥchẽ ) for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity ( kvāpāḥdyaḥ ). Instead of a kvāḥpāḥchẽ , a small temple is built in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard (called kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ ), and a statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined inside its sanctum. The temple is plastered with cement and capped by a caitya as its pinnacle. A stone toraṇa on which the images of Five Buddhas (Pañcabuddha) have been carved, is installed above the entrance to the sanctum. An additional stone statue of Akṣobhya which is slightly bigger than the main one is installed behind the main statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum. No one living in the Bāhāḥ’s premises knows about this additional Akṣobhya statue. A Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala has been established right in front of the kvāḥpādegaḥ’s entrance. The inscription on the Dharmadhātu is broken, thus the date of its establishment can not be ascertained. Next to the kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ is another small temple, which houses some Amitābha statues. Therefore, local residents call it Amitābha Mandira. Further, Pruscha (P-240) erroneously mentions this temple (Amitābha Mandira) as the kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ of Vasu Bāhāḥ. No documented evidence has so far traced out to date the initial construction of Vasu Bāhāḥ. Śākya (1994, 110) mentions that leftover bricks after the renovation of Mahābuddha Mandira ( LAL2340 ) in 1938 CE (1058 NS) were used to construct this Bāhāḥ. Therefore, we can assume that it was built around that time. However, local residents claim that it was built before the 1934 CE (1990 VS) earthquakes. The structure of the kvāḥpāḥdya and Amitābha Mandira also suggest that this Bāhāḥ is relatively new. A family of the Mahābū clan from Mahābuddha Mandira used to run and maintain the Bāhāḥ including the performance of the daily and anniversary rituals. After this family left the place some time ago, these rituals came to an end.

label: Majāḥdegaḥ (built sometime between seventeenth and eighteenth century)
description: Majāḥdegaḥ is a caitya standing on a steep slope to the south of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ ( KIR0001 ). It is built atop four-layered stone plinth. Unlike many other caityas in Kirtipur, the plinths of Majāḥdegaḥ are larger in size. Its topmost plinth is entirely made of stones. The local residents believe that these plinths must have been raised to build a temple,however no temple was ever built. For this reason, they refer to it as Majāḥdegaḥ, meaning incomplete temple . However, there is no evidence to verify these assumptions. Images of Tārā and Buddha are carved on four cardinal directions of the caitya , in accordance with the traditions. Besides these images, some smaller icons of other deities (similar to the ones carved on Yatālibi Caitya ( LAL2250 ) and found in Micchu Bāhāḥ ( LAL1100 )) are also carved on it (cf. Ś. Śre ṣṭ ha VS 2057, 64). Above these statues, a dome, harmikā, thirteen bhuvanas, and āmalaka motifs are carved. There is no evidence to date the initial construction of this monument. However, the motifs carved on the caitya suggest that it was perhaps built sometime between seventeenth and eighteenth century. It is probable that someone from the Vajrācārya castes living around this caitya might have constructed it. In 1990s, an iron sheet was welded around this caitya for its protection ( Shokoohy and others 2014, 313). The Kirtipur Municipality renovated its plinths in 2010 CE. There is no gu ṭ hī associated to this caitya . Even the elders of the area cannot recall any religious, social, or cultural activity (other than Bāhāḥ Cāḥ Hilegu) that used to be organised here.

label: Kusi Bāhāḥ (ca. 17th-18th Cen.)
description: Kusi Bāhāḥ is one of the branches ( kacā ) of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ ( KIR0002 ), located at Kusicā, to the southwest of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ premises. Kusi Bāhāḥ is also known by its Sanskrit name, Mahendrakīrti Vihāra, and (cf. Ś. Śre ṣṭ ha VS 2057, 69). Locke (1985, 182) mention it as Mahākīrti Vihāra. The bāhāḥ is accessible after walking down a flight of fifteen staircases through the ground floor of a private residential building. From the outside of this building, it is hard to assume that there is a bāhāḥ behind it. This could be the reason why Karl Pruscha was not able to locate and include this bāhāḥ in his inventory (published in 1975 CE). The bāhāḥ has a rectangular courtyard and its dya ḥchẽ (main shrine) faces northeast. The door of the dya ḥ chẽ is intricately carved, however, it lacks a tora ṇ a . Instead of a tora ṇ a , an image of Vajrasattva is carved on the door’s upper part. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated as the kvāpādya ḥ ( bāhāḥ’ s primary deity) inside the dyaḥchẽ’s sanctum . There used to be a mural on the wall inside the sanctum, however, it is completely destroyed. The dya ḥchẽ has a pasukājhyā ḥ (traditional wooden window) and an āgaṃ (shrine for the bāhāḥ ’s esoteric deity) on its first floor. Cakrasaṃvara is consecrated in the āga ṃ (based on a personal conversation with a local resident, from a Vajrācārya caste, male, age 56). Originally, the roof of the dya ḥchẽ was tiled with jhĩga ṭ ī. After it started leaking, the responsible Vajrācārya clan replaced it with corrugated pewter sheets in 2001 CE. A Śikharakūṭa Caitya is established in the middle of the bāhāḥ courtyard. There is no evidence to date the bāhāḥ ’s initial construction. The wood carving on the dya ḥ chẽ can be dated from the seventeenth and eighteenth century. A Vajrācārya family, residing in front of the bāhāḥ, are members of the saṅgha of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ, and responsible for maintaining the Bāhāḥ and carrying out the daily and other rituals. They believe that one of their ancestors constructed it. Two Śākya families, who are not members of the sa ṅgha of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ, perform their initiation ( bare chuigu ) ceremonies here. These families moved to Kirtipur some generations back and the Vajrācāryas of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ gave them the permission to use Kusi Bāhāḥ for their initiation ceremonies (cf. Locke 1985, 182). Every year, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the main gate of the bāhāḥ is open for twenty-four hours to allow the local community members to worship the kvāpādya ḥ . On other days, the main gate and the sanctum entrance are kept locked.

label: Yākaḥ Phalcā (ca. 18th cent. CE)
description: Yākaḥ Phalcā is located to the south of Gaṇeśa Mandira ( LAL0157 ) in Om Bāhāḥ Ṭola. The Phalcā is open to the north and west, with just one bay on each side. A single-bayed structure is called y ākaḥ in Newari and the Phalcā is named accordingly. The Phalcā has three carved columns and six struts. The roof is sloping down to the northern and western sides. There is an empty niche on the eastern wall of the Phalcā. According to local residents, the previous Phalcā building had a niche on the same the wall of the same direction and there were statues of Nārāyaṇa and Umāmaheśvara in the niches, which were lost before some decades. A small Gaṇeśa shrine stands next to Yākaḥ Phalcā, towards the south. It is still worshipped. No historical record is available to date the Phalcā. However, according to the local Śreṣṭha community made it around 250 years before. In the 1934 earthquakes, the building collapsed. It was then reconstructed (n.d.). In 1989, local residents demolished the crumbling structure and in 2019, the Lalitpur Municipality reconstructed it with the help of seven lakh Nepali rupees. An electric power pole stands behind the Phalcā and quasi-encroached the building. Every year on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of the Bhādra, an image of Yamāḥdyaḥ (Indra) is exhibited on top of an erected pole and on the 13th day, samaybaji (a ritual snack) is distributed. On the 4th day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the images are taken down. In earlier times, similar six images of Yamāḥdyaḥ were exhibited.

label: Bhulukā (Bhulukhā) Degaḥ aka Santāneśvara Mahādeva (supposedly built during the reign of King Prtāpa Malla [1639 – 1674 CE])
description: Bhulukā (Bhulukhā) Degaḥ, locally known as Santāneśvara Mahādeva, is located at the Yatkhā Ṭola, Naradevi. Since Pruscha (1975, 42) named it as Bhulukā Degaḥ, it is probable that the temple became popular as Santāneśvara Mahādeva only after 1975 CE. This is a three-storied tiered temple with jhĩga ṭ ī tiled roofs. The wooden elements used in the temple exhibit a sophisticated craftmanship. Its sanctum can be reached after climbing a flight of stairs since it is elevated on a two-level plinth. The ground floor has a portico supported by twelve wooden pillars (a set of four pillars in each cardinal direction). Pruscha (ibid.) recorded fifty-two struts on which various images of Śiva, Śakti, griffins, and alike have been carved. A Śivaliṅga, wrapped in a silver sheet, is consecrated inside the sanctum. There are statues of numerous deities established inside the wall niches of the sanctum. During its renovation in 2001 CE (VS 2058), all of the existing wooden elements of the temple, except for the rotten and degraded ones, were used. Thus, the temple retains its authenticity. There are no evidence to appoint the initial construction of the temple. However, local residents believe that Lamba Karṇa Bhaṭṭa, the dīk ṣā guru of King Pratāpa Malla (1639 – 1674 CE) built the temple. A huge aniconic stone can be seen on the northern side of the temple. Locals worship it as Bhairava. It is said that Bhairava including the Eight Mother Godesses ( a ṣṭ amāt ṛ kā ) was invoked in many places when the city of Kathmandu was founded. This aniconic stone is one of them and also referred to as a protector ( dikpāla ). According to a local resident (one of the descendants of Lamba Karṇa Bhaṭṭa, Śarmā, male, age 50) the head of Bhairava is buried underneath the ground since devotees should not look at his ferocious face directly. In the past, the aforementioned Bhaṭṭa family was responsible for the daily rituals and maintenance of the temple. However, an Upādhyāya caste priest performs the daily ritual in the present-day. A huge bonfire is lit in front of the temple on the day of the Śivarātrī. Mondays of the month of Śrāvana witness a multitude of devotes in the temple. Usually, childless couples perform a special ritual, wishing for offspring.

label: Tana Bāhāḥ
description: Tana Bāhā located in Caṃki Ṭola, is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). It has no proper shrine to house its principal deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ) Akṣobhya Buddha. Therefore, the deity is kept inside a simple cement plastered structure (locally called kvāḥpādegaḥ ) which is capped by a caitya . A dharmadhātujinālaya caitya is established in the courtyard. No documented evidence is so far traced out to date the Bahā’s initial construction. A narration is circulated amongst the local residents that it was built by certain Śreṣṭhas (Cipālu). The Bāhāḥ got destroyed due course of time and turned into ruins, which was then converted into a female toilet. Once upon a time, a person called Vidyālala Tāmrākāra experienced with his extraordinary sniffing capacity that something important and archeologically valuable is buried underneath the toilet (cf. H. Śākya 1994, 124). The Bāhāḥ’s remnants were found after the site was excavated and it was then rebuilt by Harṣa Bahādura Śākya, a resident of Oṃ Bāhāḥ in NS 1069 (1948 CE). After it was restored, he provided this place for the nuns who practise Sthavīravāda (vernac. Therāvāda) Buddhism. It is called Jayamaṅgala Vihāra since then. The Bāhāḥ is still inhabited by such nuns and the decedents of Harṣa Bahādura Śākya have been performing the daily rituals here. [1] Footnotes ^ Although the ritual is called daily ‘ nitya’ thus needs to be performed every day, they perform it only after certain intervals.

label: Kvātha Bāhāḥ
description: Kvātha Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). It is located on the way to Thainā Ṭola from Saugah. The Bāhāḥ’s shrine for the principal deity ( dyaḥchẽ ) is not in front of its main east-facing gate but faces north. Unlike other Bāhāḥs, its premises are not in a square shape but in an elongated rectangular shape that stretches from north to south. This was not always the case. The Bāhāḥ’s old structure can be seen in the historical photos published by Pruscha (1975,199). It shows intricately designed timber posts on the ground floor of the dyaḥchẽ and equally beautiful trikhājhyāḥ on the first. The statue of the esoteric deity ( āgãdyaḥ ), which used to be located on the first floor, is now stolen. At present, the Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ has been completely privatized and is replaced by a residential house. Similarly, the phalcā on the right and left side of the main Bāhāḥ entrance is merged into the private house. It is difficult to ascertain which deity was housed as the Bāhā’s principal deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ) because of the theft of the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’s icon. However, the members of the saṅgha mention that the icon of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, made with sandalwood, was consecrated as the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ . Based on this belief, a stone icon of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara is placed where the old dyaḥchẽ used to be. The icon of Triratnas is placed on top of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara’s statue. Locke (1985, 112), however, mentions that it is Akṣobhya, and not Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, established as the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ , and that kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’s icon was mistakenly positioned in the east. There is no inscriptive evidence about the Bāhāḥ’s construction date and its benefactor. The Sanskrit name of this Bāhāḥ is Kuṭusiṃha Vihāra. Another Bāhāḥ, Jothā Bāhāḥ, is adjacent to the Kvātha Bāhāḥ. The local residents believe that Kuṭusiṃha made this Bāhāḥ after his brother, Jōdhāju, constructed the Jothā Bāhāḥ. There is no independent saṅgha of the Bāhāḥ. Both Jothā Bāhāḥ and Kvātha Bāhāḥ are members of one saṅgha . A single temple caretaker ( dyaḥpāḥlāḥ ) performs the daily worship for both the Bāhāḥs. A Śākya family in Patan, members of this saṅgha , goes by the name of Narsingh Khalaḥ. Anniversary worship ( varṣavardhana ) of both of these Bāhāḥs used to happen on the same day. With the extinction of the Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ , the anniversary worship has also vanished. There is a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya built in NS 980 (1860 CE) on the Bāhāḥ’s premises.

label: Gaṇeśa Mandira
description: As it the case of most of the Gaṇeśa Mandiras in the Kathmandu Valley, this Mandira, too, faces, south. The local residents of Tyāgala Ṭola worship this Gaṇeśa as their area deity ( sthāna ). It is built in a pagoda-style and has three storeys. The main door to the sanctum is flanked by a pair of lions, and an artistically carved toraṇa with the images of Gaṇeśa (in the centre) and two people playing the musical instrument mṛdaṅga (in the left and right) is kept above the door. The images of Śiva, Gaṇeśa, and Mātṛkā Goddesses have been carved on the struts supporting the roofs. The last roof of the temple is metal tiled, however, the first and second roofs are tiled with jhĩgaṭī bricks. The photograph published by Pruscha (1975, p. 189) shows an additional pinnacle erected on the roof of the second floor. However, this pinnacle is not there anymore. No documented evidence is so far traced out which records the date of the temple’s initial construction. The date inscribed on the toraṇa in Nepāla Calendar Era could be the date of the initial construction. However, since the middle numeral of this date is defaced, its exact dating remains obscure. Pruscha (1975, p. 189) has mentioned that a guṭhī was established in NS 768 (1648 CE) to sponsor the daily and occasion rituals for this temple. He also informs us that the struts supporting the roofs were carved in NS 863 (1743 CE). Since he does not validate this information through any documented evidence, its authenticity remains questionable. An inscription from NS 853 (1733 CE) is kept inside the sanctum. It records about the establishment of a guṭhī that is responsible to sponsor the rituals for the caitya erected in front of this Gaṇeśa Mandira. The Mandira was renovated in VS 2060 (2003 CE) by the Department of Archelogy (source: Local knowledge, a resident of the area, Maharjana, male, age 49). The specific iconographical features of the Gaṇeśa statue [1] of this temple suggest that it is one of the oldest Gaṇeśas from the Kathmandu Valley dating back from the 5 th to 7 th century. There are three separate guṭhī s of Jyāpus, Mulmīs, and Bārāhīs of Tyāgala Ṭola related to this temple. The Jyāpus’ guṭhī sponsors ritual worship to Gaṇeśa on the day called Picāśa Caturdaśī followed by an animal sacrifice. The Mulmīs’ guṭhī worship Gaṇeśa on the day of Indrajātrā procession and Piśāca Caturdaśī and displays a metal Gaṇeśa statue in the temple for the public, which is also followed by an animal sacrifice. The Bārāhī’s gūṭhī too organises special worship for Gaṇeśa every year, on the day of Kuśe Aũśī followed by the sacrifice of a he-goat. In addition to these guṭhīs , a separate guṭhī of the Jyāpus of Tyāgala Ṭola too places a toraṇa above the main statue in the sanctum and displays it publicly twice a year. Footnotes ^ For example, it has two arms, a big belly, is not adorned with pieces of jewellery, is in the ardhaparyaṅka position, its trunk is slightly twisted to the right and it is not accompanied by other statues, such as his family members and transporter (see Khanāla VS 2074, 163 for the iconographical features of the old Gaṇeśa statues in the Kathmandu Valley).

label: Jena Bāhāḥ (ca. 15th cent. CE)
description: Jena Bāhāḥ, also known as Śrī Jñāna Nāma Vihāra, is located on the southern side of Jena Bāhāḥ Ṭola in front of the Gaṇeśa Mandira ( LAL0270 ). The courtyard can be accessed by passing through a metal door. The main structure of the bāhāḥ has mostly collapsed. Its foundations as well as wooden decorative elements are scattered around the site. The main structure on the left side of the metal door has been destroyed and is fenced off with CGI sheets. The square courtyard has a teliya tiled floor and contains a Licchavi caitya , a dharmadhātu maṇḍala at the southeastern corner and a Kṛṣṇa shrine with a brick dome at the center. To the south, one can also find a Durgā shrine raised on a platform 90 cm in height. This bāhāḥ is a branch of Hakha Bāhāḥ ( LAL0390 ). The building lacks a dyaḥchẽ , something which is normally a major feature of such bāhāḥ. Local people say that it was probably destroyed during the 1934 earthquake and never reconstructed. Locke (1985, 152) assumes that the bāhāḥ was abandoned after the earthquake. Later, Pradhānas, non-Buddhist Newar families from Kathmandu, bought the surrounding lands and constructed houses upon it. These buildings now surround the bāhāḥ area. There is no inscription at the site through which one could date the monument. Locke (1985, 154) argues that this branch predates the transfer of Hakha Bāhāḥ from its original place to its present location. This move took place during the reign of Siddhi Narasiṃha Malla (1620-1661). The Licchavi caitya in the bāhāḥ's courtyard supports this hypothesis.

label: Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira
description: Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira (Temple) is located behind the waterspout at the Guitaḥ Ṭola, and faces west. Generally, each Newar city quarter ( ṭola ) in the Kathmandu Valley has one Gaṇeśa temple, but there are two at the Guitaḥ Ṭola. The Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Temple was constructed from the Guṭhī comprising Śākyas and Maharjana caste members of the Ṭola. This one-storey Temple stands on a relatively tall plinth and is tiled with jhĩgaṭīs . The roof is capped by a metal pinnacle which is flanked by a pair of metal flags. A long metal banner ( patāḥ ) connected to the base of the pinnacle is hanging down up to the eves board. The door to the sanctum is capped by a carved wooden toraṇa and is flanked by a pair of lions. A dancing Gaṇeśa image is carved on the middle of the toraṇa and a Buddha image is carved on either side of Gaṇeśa. The sanctum of the Temple houses a stone statue of Gaṇeśa whose head is capped by a metal crown ( mukuṭa ) . L. Bangdel (1995, 230) has dated this statue to the 18 th century CE. There are some other statues established on the plinth of the Temple. Among them, the Śiva statue (LAL2030-010), which Bangdel (1995, 229) has identified as Viṣṇu, is said to be from the 14 th century CE. The statue of Viṣṇu (LAL2030-012) is dated to 15 th Century CE, and the statue of Umāmaheśvara (LAL2030-009) is said to be from the 17 th century CE (cf. Bangdel L. 1995, 229). Moreover, there is also a Sarasvatī statue (LAL2030-011) established in 1775 CE (NS 895) by a certain monk īndrajyoti. We have no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple. In 2008 CE (VS 2065), it was reconstructed with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality. The above mentioned Guṭhī currently (as of June 2021) has nine members (two Śākyas and seven Maharjanas). On the day of the Gũlā Pāru (the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra), the Guṭhī members place a brass Gaṇeśa statue in front of the main statue inside the sanctum for public display and worship it. A similar ritual is conducted also on the day of the Indra Jātrā Festival. On this day, samaybaji is offered to the deity.

label: Licchavi Caitya and statue of Buddha
description: This group of three objects is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ). The brick pedestal supports a massive stone slab (131cm x 62 cm), upon which the Licchavi Caitya, the Buddha statue and the dome fragment have been loosely placed. This Caitya was constructed some time in the Licchavi period and stands testament to the antiquity of the Bungamati settlement. The Licchavi Caitya is eroded, slightly damaged and missing its finial. Parts of the right hand and leg of the Buddha statue have broken off, most of the nimbus is missing and the damaged head has been patched up with cement mortar. The dome fragment is missing its finial and its lower part sits to the right of the statue. This collection of items was obviously quite recently assembled, and it is not known where the large stone base came from. Locals worship the Caitya during their morning visit to the temples. Besides that, other regular worships are not observed at this Caitya.

label: Pānda Bāhāḥ (1877 CE)
description: Pānda Bāhāḥ is located at Ghavāḥ Nani in Lukhusi Ṭola. Unlike most of the bāhāḥs in Patan, this one belongs to the Maharjanas, and not to the Vajrācāryas or Śākyas. Therefore, it has neither a shrine ( kvāḥpāḥchẽ ) for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ), nor a saṅgha. A small shrine is built in the south-western corner of the Ghavāḥ Nani. The bell-shaped shrine is painted in white, capped by a caitya -shaped pinnacle, and encircled by the serpents ( nāga ). A stone statue of Akṣobhya flanked by Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara is enshrined inside the shrine’s sanctum sanctorum as kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ. A Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla statue are installed in the Bāhāḥ premises. Pānda Bāhāḥ was built in NS 997 (1877 CE) by Kiṣṇa (text: Kṛṣṇa) Maharjana and his wife Tuyu (Lakṣmīdevī) living in Lukhusi Ṭola. They also established the Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya in the Bāhāḥ premises and formed a guṭhī to worship it in NS 1000 (1880 CE). The decedents of the Bāhāḥ’s founders (especially three families) are still performing the daily rituals. The anniversary celebration of the Bāhāḥ takes places every year, on the full moon day of Āśvina.

label: Jom Bāhāḥ
description: Unlike many smaller bāhāḥs in Patan, Jom Bāhāḥ is neither a branch of any major bāhāḥ nor does it belong to the Vajrācāryas or Śākyas. It is a private Bāhāḥ of Śilpakāras ( Lvahaṃkaḥmi ), who are the stone workers. This Bāhāḥ is, in fact, an āgachẽ for the Śilpakāras. Therefore, they prefer to call it āgaṃchẽ , but not Bāhāḥ. Locke (1985, 138-140) and Pruscha (1975, P-268) mention that this is called Jagata Kalyāṇa Vihāra in the Sanskrit language, however, the local residents argue that its Sanskrit name is Viśvakramā Avatāra Vihāra. A Yogāmbara statue is enshrined on the Bāhāḥ’s first floor inside the sacred and secret shrine ( āgama ). Those who are not initiated ( dīkṣā ) into the tradition are not allowed to enter the āgama . A large window capped by a toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya flanked by serpent girls is carved can be seen on the first floor. The Bāhāḥ’s sanctum is on the ground floor where an idol of Akṣobhya has been enshrined as kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ . [1] A stone Dharmadhātu Maṇdala [2] is erected in front of the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ . The door to the sanctum is flanked by Gaṇeśa, Candra, Mañjuśrī and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara (to the right), and Mahākāla and Sūrya (to the left) and is capped by a stone toraṇa on which the images of Pañcabuddhas and Tārā have been carved. A stone statue of Nāmasaṃgīti is kept above the toraṇa . A Śikharakūṭa Caitya, two Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalas, and a statue of Śivapārvatī are established in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard. The local residents believe that King of Patan, Siddhinarasiṃha Malla (r. 1620 – 1661) brought the Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas to Patan in order to make them construct temples and statues etc. in his kingdom. Sometime later, they (Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas) built two āgamas and started living permanently in Patan. Locke (1985, 138) has mentioned a copper-plate inscription recording the date of the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction, however, no such inscription is in the Bāhāḥ at present. The earliest reference to this Bāhāḥ can be found on a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 778 (1658 CE). [3] Four Śākya clans (Khicā, Hvakhāḥ, Yākaḥ, and Katilāḥ Khalas) are the members of this Bāhāḥ. Previously, they used to perform the daily rituals turn by turn. However, at present, a Vajrācārya from Mikhā Bāhāḥ has been appointed for such rituals. [4] The Vajrācārya priest worships Yogāmbara enshrined in the āgama every year, on the 14 th lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phāguna. Further, disipūjā is celebrated on the 11 th of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa. Although this Bāhāḥ was initially built by the Śilpakāras, it is also shared by the Sthāpitas. Its digi , too, is divided into two parts. The western part of the Bāhāḥ belongs to the Sthāpitas and its eastern part to the Śilpakāras. Footnotes ^ The Akṣobhya statue is dressed in a metal lhegā . ^ The date NS 795 (1675 CE) is inscribed on the Dharmadhātu (see the object LAL2680-011 below). ^ The manuscript records the name of a person (Siddhi Bhāro) who is a member of Oṃ (text: Jom) Bāhāḥ (cf. Rājavaṃśī 2041, 75). ^ He receives a monthly enumeration of 3500 rupees.

label: Guitaḥ Caitya 1 (built before 13th century)
description: Guitaḥ Caitya 1 is located in the vicinity of the Mū Guitaḥ Bahī ( LAL1980 ). It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the cardianal directions. Statues of the Four Buddhas have been placed in these niches. The main deity, Akṣobhya is placed in the southern niche with a lotus in front of him. The diameter of the single plinth drum is 670 cm, and the dome on of it has a diameter of 565 cm. Above the dome is a harmikā based on a square plan measuring 193 cm in width and 110 cm in height. There are thirteen steps or tiers above the harmikā and a ring of āmalaka around the central pillar ( yaṣṭi ). The finial is covered by a gilded parasol ( chatra ) with a pinnacle. A date (NS 368) has been inscribed on the stone pedestal. For safety reason, the statue has been cased inside an iron fence. A stone mandaḥpāḥ lies on the ground in front of the statue. The image of Amitābha that was previously established inside the western niche was stolen in 1984, and a new image of the same deity was installed immediately after this. A statue of Amoghasiddhi is enshrined on the northern niche. The eastern niche of the Guitaḥ Caitya 1 houses a broken statue of Buddha, probably Ratnasambhava. Its right hand and its left thumb are both fragmented. L. Bangdel (1995, 229) has dated this statue back to ca. 13th century. The caitya is painted in white lime and its dome is topped with a harmikā upon which the vajradṛṣṭi eyes and ūrṇā have been painted. These paintings can be found on all four sides; they symbolise nobility and illumination.

label: Harṣa Bāhāḥ (built in 1858 CE)
description: Harṣa Bāhāḥ is a private Bāhāḥ built by Harṣanarasiṃha Śākya from Haḥkhā Ṭola, Patan in 978 NS (1858 CE). He was a saṅgha member of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, commonly known as Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra. He did not only built this Bāhāḥ, but also established an esoteric deity ( āgamadevatā ) and Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya in its premises. The house for the Bāhāḥ’s principal deity ( kvāḥpāchẽ ) has two stories and faces east. [1] The place for Bāḥā’s esoteric deity ( āgama ) and sanctum are located on its first [2] and second floor, respectively. The door to the sanctum is crowned with a toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya (in the middle), and Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara (on the right and left) have been carved. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum as the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity ( kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ ). [3] Further, a Balabhadra statue made of stone is installed in front of the primary deity. Jīvadhanasiṃha (probably a family member of Harṣanarasiṃha Śākya) offered a metal vajra to the Bāhāḥ in 984 NS (1864 CE). Harṣanarasiṃha also established a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in the courtyard in 985 NS (1865 CE). The kvāḥpāchẽ was renovated in VS 2049 (1993 CE). Harṣa Bāhāḥ is maintained and run by three families. Each saṅgha member from these three families is responsible to carry out the daily rituals for a month. The Bāhāḥ’s anniversary is on every tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha. On this day, the annual death rite ( śrāddha ) is also performed to commemorate the deceased elders ( āḥju-aji ). Footnotes ^ Its roof is tiled with the jhĩgaṭī bricks, is capped by a caitya shaped pinnacle and is supported by the plain struts. ^ A trikhā window capped by a wooden toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya is carved, can be seen in this floor. ^ The statue faces east.

label: Cyāsal Phalchā 4
description: This Phalchā is located at the eastern part of the Cyāsal square next to Aśoka Stūpa Phalcā ( LAL4155 ). The whole building was rebuilt in concrete some time in the 1990s.

label: Licchavi Caitya
description: This Caitya is located to the south-west of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) of Bungmati. Bungamati is one of the oldest settlements in the Kathmandu Valley. This monument was constructed in the Licchavi period and stands testament to the antiquity of the settlement. The upper section of the Caitya was placed upon an unusually shaped brick and cement pedestal some time before 1990. Since then, the stone finial has separated from the structure and is now lying in pieces on top of the dome, which is also broken. The stone pavement around the Caitya was removed following the 2015 earthquake. The upper part of the Caitya has four small empty niches, each of which are surmounted by images of Kīrtimukha. Locals worship the Caitya during their morning visit to the temples. Besides that, other regular worships are not observed at this Caitya.

label: Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya (1863 CE)
description: This caitya displays five layers of motifs (lotus, jewel, water, fire and thunderbolt) upon its upper part, and contains images of four Buddhas and four Tārās in the four cardinal directions and corners respectively. The seats of the deities are clad in brass, as are the toraṇa above them. These images are tied to iron rods to protect them against theft. The caitya 's dome ( garbha ) and harmikā have been joined together using cement plaster, and the finial is already broken. Statues of the 13 donors are located on the southern face of vedikā alongside an inscription that records the construction date of the caitya .

label: Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandir (built in 1718 CE)
description: This śikhara -styled Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira is located in the Bāghabhairava Temple complex ( KIR0004 ). It has four doors, each crowned with a stone t oraṇa , however, the sanctum is only accessible through the one which faces west. The remaining three which face east, north, and south, are false doors. [1] The temple is stone-built and stands on a two-layered plinth. The bell-shaped roof of the temple is capped by a jvālā nhyākaṃ , functioning as its pinnacle. The present stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara, consecrated inside the sanctum, was installed in 1984 CE after the old one was stolen (cf. Ś. Śre ṣṭ ha VS 2057,43). An inscription records that Siddhirāma Bhāro and his wife Gaṃgāmayi, residents of Kirtipur, built this temple and consecrated a stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara inside its sanctum in 1718 CE (NS 838). A statue of this couple is installed in front of the temple. The inscription further mentions that they also established a guṭhī having endowed five ropanīs of land in order to maintain the temple and carry out the daily rituals. However, there is no information about the guṭhī and the land. Even the local community elders are not aware of any guṭhī or land related to this temple. The priest of Bāghabhairava Temple performs the daily rituals. The Department of Archaeology cleaned and repaired the Bāghabhairava Temple complex in around 2007 CE including the Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira. Footnotes ^ The door in the north façade has an inscription recording the initial construction of the Temple. The second inscription found inside the sanctum is not related to this Temple.

label: Ī Bahī Vãtā Vihāra (ca. 17th cent. CE)
description: Ī Bahī Vãtā Vihāra, also named Syõ Bahī ("ruined monastery"), is located to the north of Yampi Mahāvihāra in front of the northern Aśoka Stūpa. The courtyard with three shrines and three caityas is supposed to be a branch of the Yampi Mahāvihāra. The Bahī area measures 21m x 30 m. The sunken courtyard is 82 cm below floor level, paved with flagstone tiles and measuring 10 m x 24 m. It is also home to three caitya s . The southernmost Caitya is a v ajradhātu caitya , while two other are śikharakūṭa caityas. To the east of the sunken courtyard, one can find three roofed shrines for the deities each Caitya facing west. The three structures are similar and measure 3.3 x 3.8 m. Local inhabitants worship these three small shrines as three different vihāras . Inside the shrines are three newly made stone images of Akṣobhya Buddha. Pruscha (1975, 209) and Locke (1985, 205) wrote about this monument, and it seems that some remnants of the vihāra were still present at their time. However, there are some contradictions in their descriptions. Pruscha writes that bronze images of Dīpaṅkara were enshrined in the temple sanctum dated 1672 CE (NS 792). Locke states that "the northernmost shrine contains an image of Akṣobhya flanked by an image of Praj̃nāpāramitā on his right and one of Avalokiteśvara on his left; the central shrine has an image of Akṣobhya flanked by Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara on his right and Prajñāpāramitā on his left. The southern shrine has a headless image of Akṣobhya”.

label: Trivikrama Viṣṇu Mandira (c. 18th cent. CE)
description: Trivikrama Viṣṇu temple is located at Haugaḥ Ṭola, in front of the Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ ( LAL2670 ). This temple is on the left side of the road that runs from Mangal Bazar to Lagankhel. It is built upon a double plinth and the principal façade is to the west. The temple can be accessed by climbing a narrow flight of stairs guarded by two small stone lions. The main façade has a single carved door on the ground floor and a surmounting toraṇa supported by the door posts. The other three walls have been left blank and have no openings. The first floor level is distinguished by beautifully carved wooden cornice bands. Four carved windows on the first floor are flanked by two small aedicules, and these can be found on each side of the temple. The overhanging roof is covered with traditional jhĩgaṭī tiles and supported by the carved struts. Some of these struts are missing and have been replaced by plain ones. The temple structure's bell-shaped dome structure above the first roof is unique. This towering octagonal dome has been plastered with lime and has a gilded finial with single layer of āmalaka . Sixteen struts support the roof of this two-storied temple. Among them, six older struts display carvings of various incarnations of Viṣṇu. The other, newer struts are plain and were fixed in place after the original ones were stolen. A stone statue of Trivikrama Viṣṇu is enshrined in the sanctum of the temple. This form of Viṣṇu is also called Viṣṇu Vikrānta or Vāmana. Viṣṇu has an aura behind his face and is wearing a crown, earrings, a necklace, arm jewelry and a bracelet. He has eight hands, and holds a sword, a wheel and a punishing stick in three of his right hands. The fourth right hand is performing the gesture of varada. On his left, he holds a shield, a conch and a club, whilst his fourth hand is performing a tarjanī gesture. His left leg rises up to the level of his head. The Śrīmadbhāgavatamahāpurāṇa (8.18) states that Viṣṇu descended as the Vāmana to restore the authority of Indra over the heavens, as it had been taken by the benevolent Asura King Mahābali. Vāmana, a dwarf Brahmin, went to the king to request land that he could set his foot upon for three paces. Mahābali promised to provide him with this amount of land. Vāmana then grew himself to gigantic proportions and strode over the three worlds. With his first step, he covered the space from heaven to earth, and with his second he strode from the earth to the netherworld. WIth these steps, Mahābali's realms were covered entirely, and there was no space for him to take his third step. Unable to fulfill his promise, Mahābali offered his head for the third, and so Vāmana placed his foot on Mahabali's head. No inscription or any other historical document recording the initial construction of the temple could be uncovered. Relying on the architecture of the temple as a dating method, Jośī (VS 2029, 58) assumes that this temple was constructed in the 18th century. Nowadays, the temple is in a neglected condition. There are shops on the temple's plinths, the sanctum is used as a storage room, and the key to the door is in the possession of the shopkeepers.

label: Vajradhātu Caitya (ca. 19th cent. CE)
description: Local residents refer to this Caitya as Ta ḥ Ga ḥ Bhaw āndya ḥ. According to H. Śākya’s (1993, 82) classification, this Caitya is a Vajradhātu Caitya. The Caitya has niches on its eastern, southern, western and northern sides which contain stone statues of Akṣobhaya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amogasiddhi respectively. The stone inscription attached to the western platform has been severely damaged. The Caitya has a gu ṭhī that consists of five members from the Jyapū community. They have been taking care of the monument and conduct its yearly religious activities.

label: Thyākā Bāhāḥ (1895 CE)
description: Thyākā Bāhāḥ is located near Naka Bahī ( LAL0880 ) to the right-hand side of the street on the way to Kvālkhu. The small courtyard of the Bāhāḥ measures 3.6 m x 3.8 m and is surrounded by residential buildings. The way to access the Bāhāḥ is not immediately obvious; one needs to pass through a shop to reach it. The courtyard is encircled by a stone plinth and a cement plastered floor. The main temple is a single storey structure built on a raised plinth that is 80 cm high. It is open to the east side, while its rear west wall is attached to the neighbouring building. The main entrance to the shrine has a toraṇa attached to its timber carved frame and is sheltered by an overhanging roof, on top of which is half-domed pinnacle. The toraṇa displays images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara. Two small niches to the south and north of the main shrine house small statues of the Buddhist deities Mañjuśrī and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara respectively. Both niches are topped with prayer wheels. A small statue of Gaṇeśa can be found on the southern wall of the courtyard. The name of the Bāhāḥ is comes from the name of the ṭola . This is an independent Bāhāḥ ; it was constructed by a member of Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra (Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ). Unlike other Bāhāḥs there is no kvāḥpāḥchẽ here. Instead, the shrine of Akṣobhya is attached to the western wall of the courtyard. Inside the sanctum, one can find a marble image of Akṣobhya sitting on two layers of lotus petals. Marble lions were placed on the both sides of the entrance. However, only the northern lion remains today (2019). Inside the courtyard, one can also find a djarmadhātujinālaya caitya (170 cm high). This was installed in 1895 (NS 1015). No inscription recording the history of the Bāhāḥ could be found.

label: Ibāḥ Bahī Dune (19th cent. CE)
description: Ibāḥ Bahī Dune Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Ibāḥ Bahī ( LAL2730 ) and is situated to its west. This Bāhāḥ can be accessed through the back door of the Ibāḥ Bahī. Alternatively, there are also other two access points: either from the southwest corner, or the northwest corner from Ibāḥ Bahī. Bhājudhana Siṃha from Ibāḥ Bahī constructed this small Bāhāḥ, and so it is also called Bhājudhanasiṃha Vihāra. The courtyard measures 4 m × 13 m and contains a shrine of Akṣobhya Buddha at its centre. The god house is attached to the western wall of the Ibāḥ Bahī, and measures 3.2 m in width and 2.1 m in depth. It is built in brick masonry and has a flat concrete slab as a roof. The main door of the structure is not centrally aligned with the shrine, and it lacks the artistic features common to Bāhāḥ. The door has some carvings, and is flanked by wall paintings of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. A small window is fixed to the left-hand side of the main door. Inside the sanctum, there is a north-facing brass image of Akṣobhya. The stone image of the deity was stolen 3-4 years ago, and this new one was installed in its place. On top of the roof, one can find a stūpa -shaped finial. Images of Hanumān and Mahākāla are attached to the wall and flank the entrance that leads to Ibāḥ Bahī. The Bāhāḥ-courtyard is paved with teliyā bricks and also contains a Pañcāvaliyukta Caitya. No inscription or other document providing information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be found. However, Pruscha (1975, 204) dates it to the 19th century.

label: Sikucā Bāhāḥ (ca. mid-17th cent. CE)
description: Sikucā Bāhāḥ, a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ), is located to the north-east corner of the Thainā crossroad. This bāhāḥ is on the way to Thainā from Saugaḥ Hiti. The bāhāḥ -courtyard is sunken and has an Aśoka Caitya at its center on the axis to the entrance and the main bāhāḥ building. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala is located to the south in front of the caitya . The western wall of the bāhāḥ is attached to a newly constructed five-storied building. Three steps guarded by two small stone lions lead up to the bāhāḥ. Its main entry door is to the north and boasts an original carved door frame with new paneled door leaves. Two small windows on either side of the door are now used as the niches for the māne ( prayer wheel). The ground floor is separated from the first floor by a band of carved timber cornice. The principal façade has a central five-fold pāsukājhyāḥ on the first floor; this is flanked by two small aedicules on either side, as is standard. Above the pasukājhyāḥ, one can find seven images of the Buddhist deities with Prajñāpāramitā to their right and Lokeśvara to their left. A projecting slanted balcony with a simple railing of vertical balusters fixed to the timber handrail can be found on the second floor. The entrance is flanked by concrete statues of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Images of the Five Buddhas, parrots, eight auspicious symbols and other motifs have been carved on the entrance.
