A small caitya flanked by two deers has been fixed above it. Passing through the entrance, one can see a statue of Gaṇeśa to the right and Mahākāla, Garuḍa and Bhīmasena to the left. All are fixed on the walls of the residential buildings. The north-facing three-storied esoteric shrine ( āgama ) of the bāhāḥ stands at the south wing of the courtyard. The pinnacle of the bāhāḥ is a stūpa which is located on the ridge of the corrugated galvanized iron sheets roofing. This roof is supported by plain struts. A metal banner hangs down from the pinnacle to the top of the pāsukājhyāḥ . The first floor houses the āgama, whilst the second floor remains empty. The toraṇa above the left window on the first floor has already been lost. The sanctum of the bāhāḥ is located on the ground floor. J. Locke (1985, 103) mentions that there was once a toraṇa with images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara above the entrance of this sanctum. However, this was stolen some years ago. The entrance is flanked by two concrete images of Lokeśvara and two prayer wheels. The steps leading to the sanctum are flanked by two stone lions and metal flags. Inside the sanctum, one can find a stone image of Akṣobhya. No inscription or other documented evidence with any information about the establishment of the bāhāḥ could be found. A legend suggests that this monastic building's statue of Akṣobhya is related to the Guji Bāhāḥ ( LAL2490 ) . The Guji Bāhāḥ complex once caught fire, and the sandalwood statue of its main deity was brought here for its protection. After the fire, in NS 1 (881 CE), a donor named Vaiśravarṇa reconstructed the bāhāḥ . People then came to this bāhāḥ to retrieve the main deity. However, they could not lift the image up; it had become fixed in its place. As such, the image became siddha (established) there, and so it was that this bāhāḥ got the name 'Siddha Bāhāḥ'. Over time, this changed into Sikucā Bāhāḥ (cf. H. Śākya 2001, 29-30). A tradition dictates that initiates of this bāhāḥ must be taken to Guji Bāhāḥ and shown the image of Akṣobhya. J. Locke (ibid.) mentions that a descendant of Abhayarāja (the man who constructed the Mahābuddha Temple ( LAL2340 )) built the Sikucā Bāhāḥ, though he does not provide any source.

label: Sijaḥ Bāhāḥ (c. early 17th cent. CE)
description: This monastic compound is a branch of the larger monastery Bu Bāhāḥ ( LAL0440 ). It has a small shrine on its western side that faces east. This shrine takes the form of a one-storey temple based on a low stone plinth. The main deity has been placed on a raised plinth 90 cm above this base plinth. The plinth has a nāgvaḥ design (quarter round) profile at its base with a band of kasimvaḥ decorative bricks above it. A line of nāgabelī can be found on the brick wall around the middle of the plinth. The edge of the plinth consists of a black stone above a layer of lotus leaf bricks that have eroded due to weather exposure. On top of this plinth is a small carved timber structure which opens up at three sides and with a rear brick wall. The sanctum has a unique pitched roof; its three tiers are plastered in lime, and the upper part has a bell-shaped design. A stūpa forms the pinnacle of the temple. In front of the temple structure and at the center of the courtyard, one can find a vajradhātu caitya built on a square plan of 386 cm. A small dharmadhātu maṇḍala (80 cm high) has been built between the caitya and the temple structure. The square courtyard measures 13.3 m x 13.3 m and is surrounded by residential buildings in all directions, with a small open space at the south-east corner. Normally, one can see images of Mahākāla and Hanumān at the gate of most bāhāḥs, however this is not the case here. There is also no toraṇa above the main shrine's entrance. Locke (1985, 159) and Vajrācārya (1993, 117) both mention that the main deity in the sanctum used to be a statue of Amitābha. However, this has been replaced by a stone statue of an eastern-facing Akṣobhya. No inscription or other document providing any further information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be uncovered. Although he cannot find hard evidence to prove his theory, Pruscha (2015, 140) argues that this monument was constructed in the 16th century. The Bāhāḥ was built by Śreṣṭhas, and Vajrācāryas from Bu Bāhāḥ used to perform the ritual worship in the shrine. The Śreṣṭha representatives bestowed lands upon the shrine to fund a guṭhī for its management ( Vajrācārya 1993, 117). Until the late 20th century, 5 pāthī of unhusked rice was collected every year for the Bāhāḥ from the harvest. Today, the situation has changed; the Bāhāḥ no longer receives income from the land and the daily ritual worship has come to an end.

label: Vajradhara Phalcā (ca. 19th cent. CE)
description: The small courtyard in which Vajradhara Phalcā is located is called Ghana Bāhāḥ ( LAL2330 ) and contains a small temple in which a new Akṣobhya Buddha image resides. The temple is flanked by two phalcās: Mahākāla Phalcā ( LAL4092 ) to the south-east and Vajradhara Phalcā to the north-west. Vajradhara Phalcā used to house a Vajradhara statue, however this was stolen around 1985. J. Locke (1985, 112) confirms that the shrine was empty upon his visit. Since the disappearance of the deity, religious activities at the Phalcā have also ceased. The stone stele located behind the stone pedestal has three lines inscribed in Sanskrit. The walls and niches were once plastered. Currently, the Phalcā is used for storing building materials for a house under construction next door. Only its stone pedestal remains.Vajradhara Phalcā is in an advanced state of decay, though it retains many of its original components such as simple carved pillars, a traditional shrine with a historic carved door, and its jingati roof tiles. However, the ridged tiles have been replaced with plain brick and the roof is leaky. The platform’s stone edge on the eastern side appears to have been well-preserved but the tile paving is badly damaged. The original entry door at the east has been replaced by a frame covered in metal.

label: Duru Bāhāḥ Nani (1677 CE)
description: Duru Bāhāḥ Nani can be accessed from the northwest corner of the Pimbahal area through a narrow alley under the residential buildings or via a narrow path to the west of the Sulima area. The main shrine has three storeys and faces east. The principal façade of the main shrine has a main door and two small latticed windows on the ground floor. A threefold pāsukājhyaḥ is on the central axis of the first floor, and has two small-carved windows on either side. Three openings can be found on the second floor above this, though they lack window shutters. The building has been reconstructed using bricks on mud mortar, and is roofed with corrugated metal sheets. Two d harmadhātu m aṇḍalas and a v ajradhātu c aitya are in line with the front of the main building. The courtyard was recently (writing in 2019) paved with hexagonal concrete blocks. Duru Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ (Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra). Rather than referring to it as a vihāra or bāhāḥ , local people call it Bhagiṃ Nani. A historical photo (see Pruscha 1975, 148) shows that main shrine of the Bāhāḥ once had a tiled roof. Locke (1985, 128) has described the toraṇa above the entrance of the sanctum as containing images of Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, and Pruscha's photo (1975, 148) confirms this. However, the toraṇa is no longer there. Entering the sanctum, one finds an east-facing image of Akṣobhya. The inscription attached to the wall to the south of the entrance informs that this vihāra was established by Ratna Vajrācārya in NS 797 (CE 1677). Locke (ibid.) writes that it was a branch of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ until 1975 and became later a branch of Guji Bāhāḥ. However, local people say that this Bāhāḥ is and has always been a branch of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ. As evidence, they mentioned that a traditional practice takes place on the 10th day of the bright half of the Kārttika. On this day, the feast of the Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ Saṅgha is organised and the bāphāḥcā offers a pumpkin to its branch monasteries among them this Bāhāḥ.

label: Caitya (1964 CE)
description: This Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and is part of a group of another four caityas and a dharmadh ātu ma ṇḍala, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira. The base structure of the Caitya is made from brick and plastered with cement mortar, however, the dome and finial are made of stone. Four Buddha statues have been placed in the niches that face each of the four cardinal directions. The Caitya was constructed in 1964. An umbrella is placed on top of the Caitya on the full moon day of Āśvina, and its anniversary worship takes place on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.

label: Gaṇeśa Shrine (c. mid- 17th cent. CE)
description: Cola Nani is located at the northern end of Bungamati. It consists of one Gaṇeśa shrine and three caityas . The shrine was built around 1973; people brought wood from the nearby forest for its construction. Before this, the Gaṇeśa shrine stood in an open space. Leaning against the back wall, Gaṇeśa's house is supported by eight plain columns and has a hip roof covered in tiles (which local residents call Chinese tiles). The Nani is also known as Gubhāḥkhyaḥ Nani due to the fact that Gubhāḥjus and Vajrācāryas live in its vicinity. Local residents say that Bandhudatta Ācārya helped King Narendradeva and Lalita Jyāpu to bring the Red Matsyendranātha to the Kathmandu Valley, and that he lived in this Nani. The Vajrācāryas living in this area therefore believe that they are the descendants of Bandhudatta.

label: Narasiṃha Mandira (1590 CE)
description: Narasiṃha Mandira was built by Purandara Siṃha, a mah āpātra of Lalitpur in NS 710 (1590 CE) in memory of his elder brother Narasiṃha Deva. It is one of the few early śikhara towers in the Valley. Although Śaiva mortuary temples are found in many places, this is said to be the first mortuary temple with a Vaiṣṇava image ( Tiwari 2013, 113). Two stone lions guard the temple and two guarding deities are installed on the top plinth. The left deity is a four-handed Garuḍa using two hands to pray and the others to hold a flower and a water vessel. The deity sitting on the right-hand side is holding a cakra (wheel), aṅkuśa (hook), gadā and pāśa (noose). Inside the sanctum, an eight-handed stone image of Narasiṃha, the fourth incarnation of Viṣṇu, stands on a pedestal holding khaḍga , cakra , vajra and gadā with his right hands and śaṅkha , pāśa , padma and aṅkuśa with his left hands. Garuḍa sits to his left and Lakṣmī is located to his right. Unlike other commonly found Narasiṃha images, this Narasiṃha is standing but is not pictured tearing apart Hiraṇyakaśipu's abdomen. The temple sits on two lower plinths and an upper plinth with porches extending in all four directions. The sanctum tapers upwards towards the śikhara . Located on the ground floor, the main sanctum can be accessed from the east side by a series of steps. Stone pillars rest on either side of the porch, though the columns attached to the walls of the sanctum are made of timber. The lintel beam is also made from timber and has layers of brick cornice above it. Four doorways can be found on each of the sanctum's walls, but the main entrance is on the eastern side. Four porches have been built to form turrets above the sanctum, and are attached to the main śikhara tower. These turrets have small openings on three of their side walls, as well as terracotta toraṇa capped by decorative brick work and a stone finial. Their walls have been plastered with lime. The main brick tower is at the centre and contains seven bands known as saptaratha . The topmost crown of the śikhara is embellished with layers of floral patterned cornices and an āmalaka plastered with lime. The pinnacle is made from stone.

label: Nāsaḥ Phalcā
description: Nāsaḥ Phalcā is a single-storey Phalcā situated in Cyāsal. It stands on the western edge of the route which leads from from Kvaylāchi (south) to the outskirts of Cyāsal (north), and its rear wall is attached to the Nāsaḥ Capāḥ. From the Phalcā, one enters into an office that is located inside but otherwise disconnected from the building of the Capāḥ, which is dedicated to Nāsaḥdhyaḥ, the god of music and dance. The first floor of the Capāḥ is located above Nāsaḥ Phalcā and is used for Hari bhajan. It was reconstructed in 2018 after being dismantled and rebuilt in 1992. None of the historic elements were preserved. The structure now has a cement roof with modern columns. Its associated groups are the Nāsaḥ Guṭhī, the Cyāsaḥ Maṃkā Khalaḥ and the Yanyā Guthi of Byañjankārs of Nhukaṃchẽnani (Mahārānī Cukaḥ).

label: Āratī Chẽ
description: Āratī Chẽ, a ceremonial rest house (capāḥ), is closely related to Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ) and located to the temple's north-west. The building's name translates as "oil lamp house" meaning "the building where oil lamps are prepared". According to local informants, the original Āratī Chẽ collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was not reconstructed until 2018. A photo taken in 1968 (published in Bungmati 1968: A Survey by Danish Architect Students , page 21) shows the building site to be empty. The 2018 reconstruction was financed by the Lalitpur Municipality and represents a hybrid structure combining traditional and modern styles and building techniques. The walls have been constructed using regular brick and are painted with surkhi (brick dust and lime mortar). Horizontal and vertical timber bands have been inserted at regular intervals as seismic strengthening devices, something that is not a traditionally found in this type of building. A concrete slab supports the open terrace. The building's main facade (which faces south) has been built in a traditional configuration whereas the facades facing west and north remain unfinished and lack the traditional overhanging roofs. Oil lamps ( āratī ) are prepared at Aratī Chẽ for ceremonial use at the Karuṇāmaya temple. The deity Buṅgadyaḥ (also known as Karuṇāmaya) is worshipped four times a day: in the early morning, at noon, in the evening and in the middle of the night. Oil lamps are offered to the deity at the end of each worship (see Locke 1985, 238 for more details). The Aratī Chẽ guṭhī is managed by a Śākya family, one of the 31 priest families of Karuṇāmaya Mandira. This family prepares the oil lamps and brings them to the temple. In the time between the building's destruction in 1934 and its reconstruction in 2018, the family prepared the oil lamps in their house.

label: Buṅga Bahī (18th cent.)
description: Buṅga Bahī, also known as Prathampura Mahāvihāra, is located at the northwestern end of Buṅgamatī. The monument can be reached from the northern gate of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira ( BUN0001 ). This bahī is in Lalitpur but is not counted among the major bahīs of the district. It is named after Buṅgamatī, but is also referred to as Prathamapura Mahāvihāra, meaning the first bahī of the area. It is under the ownership of local Śākyas. These people write their last name as Brahmācārya Bhikṣu. The bahī has four entrances, one at each of its four sides, but the eastern one forms the main entrance. The bahī's hip roof is supported by plain struts, whilst the first floor is held up by double-layered pillars. As is often the case with bahī, one can find a phucā atop its roof. However, the śivaliṅga -shaped finial sets this bahī apart from others; these structures generally have a caitya -shaped finial. A veranda surrounds the first floor of the bahī complex. Inside, an L-shaped staircase leads up to the first floor. The sanctum of the bahī is on the first floor of the western building and houses an east-facing statue of Akṣobhya. Two stone lions and two metal flags flank the entrance of the sanctum. Carved panels depicting a Gandharva, a female figure and a water vessel have been fixed on either side of the entrance. A śivaliṅga -shaped aśoka caitya stands in the courtyard. No historical record could be found with which to date the bahī . However, a local folk tale tells that Matsyendranātha was brought to the Valley and requested to live in Bungmati. However, he replied that he did not want to dwell in a place without a bahī . As a result, this bahī was constructed and the deity accepted the request to live here. According to the bahī members, this bahī was established by Dhyānacandra Miśra. Three merchant brothers from Patan, Dharmaśrī Miśra, Jñānaśrī Miśra and Dhyānacandra Miśra, spent the money they had earned through Tibetean trade to establish three bahīs . These are known as Kvanti Bahī, I Bahī and the present bahī. However, no historical record is available to verify this claim. The only inscriptions found in the bahī complex stem from the late Malla period. The bahī suffered from multiple earthquakes and has undergone reconstruction multiple times. This took place most recently in 2005 and was carried out by the Department of Archeology in Nepal. The main worship rituals that take place are the annual ritual worship of the caitya , a Vasundharā worship, a Mahākāla worship, and a srāddha (a ritual performed in honour of dead relatives) for Dhyānacandra Miśra. A guṭhī endowed with 45 ropanī of land in Bungmati and Sunaguthi was established to run the social and religious activities of the bahī ( Locke 1985 , 223). However, some of the guṭhī's lands have been privatised, and even the tenant farmers working the other lands no longer give the bahī's share to the guṭhī . The saṅgha -members of the bahī therefore rely on the collection of donations in order to fund these activities.

label: Dampāchẽ Caityas (1979 CE)
description: Two dharmadhātujinālaya caityas , commonly referred to as chaturamukha caitya (i.e a caitya which has four faces) and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala are located on the western side of the main road at Hitipusaḥ Jaḥrũ, Dampāchẽ, Sunāguthi. Four Buddha images sit on top of the upward opening lotus blossoms above a single layer of petals. These blossoms are supported by a lion throne positioned on top of a square pedestal which in turn sits upon the square plinth. A drum, a dome and a finial have been placed above the four Buddha images. The caityas are 200 cm in height. An octagonal shaped dharmadh ātu ma ṇḍala (80 cm in height) lies to their west.

label: Kani Bāhāḥ at Oku Bāhāḥ (1702 CE)
description: Kani Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260 ) and was established in 1702 (NS 822) by Devarāja Śākya. It is located at the southeast corner of Lalitpur city, on the way to Sincāhiti from Oku Bāhāḥ. This Bāhāḥ is on the fringe of the city, at the crossroad of the roads from Prayag Pokhari to Gwarko and Satdobato. It can be accessed via a carved door on the northern side of the complex. The front facade of the main door has changed and shops have been built up around it. Two doors have also been added on either side of it. The main door is accentuated by two small blind windows and carvings of deities on either side of it. Entering the door via a vestibule, one finds a colonnaded space ( phalcā ) on the second bay, as well as images of Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla and Hanumān to the left, on the eastern wall, and an image of Bhīmasena to the right, on the western wall. The Phalcā has three bays and a pair of columns ( jvaḥthā̃ ). The main courtyard is surrounded by a plinth, measures 8.85m x 8.85m, and is 45cm below the level of the Phalcā. The main sanctum building is a three-storey structure built on the southern wing of the courtyard. It has a richly carved central main door on the ground floor that is flanked by two small windows with circular lattice work on either side. The upper floor is distinguished by a band of carved timber cornice that is typical to Newar architecture. On the first floor, one can find a pasukā jhyāh with two aedicules on either side. The second floor is mainly occupied by a central slanting projected window known as gā jhyāḥ . The sanctum building has two exit doors on the ground floor; the eastern door leads to an open space to the south, while the western one is the entrance to a residential building. There are two lattice windows on the first floor and one single window on the second floor. The roof is covered with jhiṅgati tiles and has a stūpa finial on its ridge. The building now stands in the shadow of a newly constructed five-storey building behind it, i.e. to its south. The courtyard is well paved with high quality teliyā tiles. It contains a Durgatipariśodhana caitya (220cm high), a statue of some donors and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala (80cm high). These are all lined up in front of the main sanctum building. The north-facing god house of the Bāhāḥ has three storeys, though it was seriously affected by the 2015 earthquake. It can be found at the southern side of the courtyard. Its worn tiled-roof is damaged in some parts, and vegetation is growing on and through it. Although the roof is dilapidated, it is still topped by a caitya -shaped pinnacle. According to Bāhāḥ members, Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided 28 Lakh Rupees for the reconstruction of the monastery.

label: Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ (built before 1628 CE)
description: Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ is located on the southern side of Patan Darbar Square. Unlike other b āhāḥs , Haugaḥ has no affiliation with Śākyas or Vajrācāryas. Rather, it is a private Bāhāḥ belonging to the Rājakarṇikāra community. The Bāhāḥ can be accessed via the carved door located at the east wing of the monastic complex. The entry porch of the complex has four wooden pillars and is suggestive of a colonnaded phalcā with seating space added at a later date. The courtyard measures 10.0m x 9.8m and is encircled by a plinth with a depth of 1.1m. The sunken courtyard is 42cm deep and contains a dharmadhātu maṇḍala and an aśoka caitya . The sanctum building faces east and has a central main door with two stone lions guarding the steps that lead up to it. The door is surmounted by a wooden toraṇa that exhibits three eight-handed tantric deities. The façade has a tikijhyāḥ on its first floor and a trikhājhyā on the second floor. The three-storied esoteric building faces east and has a phujā above it. Four decorative struts support the sloping roof, which is clad in brass. The lower roof is covered with corrugated metal sheets and supported by six struts. Four of these display images of gods whilst the other two are decorated with flower motifs. The façade of the second floor has a carved window. Glass panes have been fixed in the window frame, and it is flanked by two tikijhyās . The first floor houses the āgama of the Bāhāḥ, and this floor also has a brass-clad trikhājhyāḥ . A brass-clad aedicule has been fixed to the right of the window and a gilded window has been installed to its left. Above the middle window, one can see a wall painting of seven tathāgatas . The sanctum of the Bāhāḥ is on the ground floor. A brass toraṇa exhibiting images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara surmounts the brass-clad entrance of the sanctum. The door is flanked by concrete images of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. An image of Mahākāla can be found to the right of this door, whilst images of Sarasvatī and Hanumān are located to its left, alongside an empty niche that represents the main deity of the āgama . Two stone lions, metal flags and hanging bells have been placed on either side of the entrance. The statue of the main deity of the Bāhāḥ, Akṣobhya, is made of stone and is adorned in lhegā . The building attached to the dyaḥchẽ to the north is used by the Sanāḥ Guṭhī, which is also called Rājakarṇikāra (Halvāī) Śaraṇa Guṭhī. The southern building attached to the sanctum belongs to the Bāhāḥ. A Buddha-statue can be found sleeping on the first floor of this house. The room is named after this statue and is known as 'Relaxing Buddha'. A p añcāvaliyukta caitya and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala have also been placed inside the room. This room is used as an office by the Rājakarṇikāra society. No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide any information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ. During the Malla period, elephants were reared at the Haugala Ṭola. This area was therefore once known as Hastināgala. The word 'Hastināgala' gradually morphed into variations such as Hātigala, Hatigla, Haugala and Haugaḥ. At that time, one of the ministers of the Malla Kings suggested he bring two Brahmins from Kannauj, India to prepare sweets for him. The king invited these two individuals and offered them land at Hastināgala Ṭola. The Brahmins were called Rājakarṇikāra. They later became integrated into the Buddhist Newar community and established their own bāhāḥ . Later, King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha allowed them to open a sweet shop near the shrine of Nārāyaṇa at the present Nārāyaṇahiṭī compound (cf. Locke 1985, 229). A dense population of Karṇikāra caste members surrounds the Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ.

label: Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ
description: Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ is located to the west of Uku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ). It is located inside an L-shaped courtyard which can be accessed through a narrow underpass by a six storied building. The bāhāḥ is on the way to Thāpāhiṭī from Mahābuddha. The main monument building is a small structure attached to a residential building to the west. It is not visible from the main entrance; one must walk to the end of the long courtyard and turn right to find an adjacent courtyard. Together, they form an open L-shaped space. Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Oku Bāhāh. The god house sits on a stone plinth raised above the ground. The main sanctum is constructed from timber and exhibits intricately carved door jambs and a toraṇa thā (the place for toraṇa ). Four corner posts have been carved to resemble the column that supports the three-tiered roofs, which in turn are covered with brass plates. The structure's pinnacle is missing. Behind the monument, there is a four-storey residential building with a projecting carved open window at the center flanked by two vertical lattice windows on either sides on the first floor. Above this, the second floor boasts a central and elaborately carved triple-opening window. The ground floor has a three-bayed colonnaded structure, and the central bay is occupied by this monument. In front of the monument, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya (2 m high) and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala (65 cm high) on a raised platform paved in stone. The structure of this bāhāḥ differs from other bāhāḥ of Patan; this bāhāḥ has no kvāḥpāḥchẽ . The brass-clad roof of the temple is supported by struts that display images of Lokeśvaras. Previously, one could find an image of Amitābha inside the temple's sanctum, but this is presently at the home of one of the main authorities of the bāhāḥ . A toraṇa above the entrance of the sanctum shows Lokeśvara with Prajñāpāramitā to her right and another Lokeśvara to her left. Śākya (1994, 118-119) writes that the sanctum also contained wall paintings of Māyādevī, Cintāmaṇi Lokeśvara, Padmasaṃbhava, Harihariharivāhanalokeśvara, Uṣṇīṣavijaya, Āryatārā, Dhvajāgrakeyūrī and the first Bhīmarathārohaṇa. However, only three of them (Uṣṇīṣavijaya, Āryatārā and Padmasaṃbhava) are still there. Bhājudhana Śākya was a member of the saṅgha of Oku Bāhāḥ and he established this bāhāḥ with help of his elder brother Bhīmarāja and other family members. Bhājudhana had shop in Tibet where he sold gold jewellery. He established this vihāra using the money he earned from his business. As a result, this vihāra is also called Hiraṇyalābha Vihāra. In NS 1027 (1907 CE), Bhājudhana established a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya in the courtyard. Two years later, he made a small god house and enshrined the image of Akṣobhya inside it.

label: Khāchẽ Bāhāḥ (1801 CE)
description: This Bāhāḥ is located in Khācheñ Ṭola between Naka Bahī and Dhalāyacā Ṭola and is a branch of the Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra. The stone-paved residential courtyard measures only 3 m x 3.2 m and can be accessed from the north, through an alley underneath a house connecting the courtyard with the Swotha street. The courtyard has a unique caitya at its center. It is one of a kind in Patan since its garbhag ṛ ha, harmikā, trayodaśabhuvana and pinnacle are all made of crystal. To the east of the Caitya, is a traditional door which still remains within the modern house fabric. The special carved timber door (missing the threshold) with an extended lintel must have been an entry to a special place related to the rituals but at present, the space is rented for commercial use. The shrine of the main deity of the Bāhāḥ is lost, and a space to the west is still empty waiting for the deity, an east-facing Akṣobhya Buddha, to return from the guthi member who took it to his home when the adjacent house was demolished. An inscription informs that Jayānanda built the Caitya in 1801 CE (NS 921). According to local informants, Jayānanda Śākya was a professional sculptor who used to make images of crystal. This crystal Caitya sits on a copper pedestal, which is shaped as a lotus with three folds of petals turned upwards. This lotus sits on a slim base that gently increases in circumference as it nears the ground. Beneath this is a double-tier rectangular stone plinth. The caitya is framed by a five-tier copper pinnacle, which is supported by four copper serpents, with their tails near the top and their heads facing downwards. It is encased in a metal cage and has a brass roof. Above the pinnacle is an unbrella ( chatra ) with five layers and which is supported by stylised snakes (nāga ) . There are four images in the four corners of the Caitya . In the southwest corner is an image of the donor (Jayānanda), and in the southeast corner is an image of Garuḍ a . Similarly, in the northwest corner there is an image of an elephant, and in the northeast corner there is an image of a lion.

label: Kapileśvara Mahādeva Mandira (built in 1690 CE)
description: Kapileśvara Mahādeva Mandira is located adjacent to the Bicche Bāhāḥ, Kathmandu. It faces west. The current stone pinnacle of the temple was installed after the previous golden one was stolen. A stone tora ṇ a featuring chepu adorns the entrance of the sanctum. A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum, and there is also an additional Śivaliṅga inside the sanctum area, its jalaharī faces east. The inscription installed to the north of the sanctum entrance informs us that it was constructed by Kaṃpālidāsa (Kapiladāsa) and his wife Māneśvarī in 1690 CE (NS 810). The inscription does not mention the caste of Kaṃpālidāsa, but local residents believe that he was from a Pradhāna caste. His family also constructed the Bicche Phalcā ( KAT0941 ) which is adjacent to the temple. Kaṃpilādāsa’s family endowed land to the temple and established a gu ṭ hī to finance the daily, annual, occasional, and other rituals. However, no official ritual activities take place in the temple in the present-day. Local community members visit the temple and worship the Śivaliṅga in early mornings. A fire oblation is performed on the day of Śrīpañcamī (Sarasvatīpūjā) in the adjacent Bicche Phalcā ( KAT0941 ). Its gu ṭ hī members also perform a special worship in this temple on that day. Reṇukā Vajrācārya, a member of the local community, has been voluntarily cleaning the temple every Tuesday.

label: Bhūkampa Smāraka (1941 CE)
description: Bhūkampa Smāraka is a stone pillar that stands at the northern end of the Patan Darbar Square and in front of the three-tiered Bhīmasena temple (LAL1380) . The stone pillar is based on a double plinth of stone, which is surrounded by a square stone paving measuring 260 cm x 260 cm. The bottom plinth (17 cm high) measures 153 cm x 153 cm whilst the top plinth (25 cm high) measures 97 cm x 97 cm. The pillar is 168 cm high and has a 40 cm square base. The pillar is tapers at the base around a height of 70 cm; above this, it is straight. The top of the pillar has small recessed motifs and has a lotus base for an image of Annapūrṇā (58 cm tall). This pillar was erected in 1941 by the people of Lalitpur in memory of the devastating 1934 earthquake and in honor of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera and his assistance. A similar kind of memorial was also established in the Bhugol Park of New Road, Kathmandu. The Patan Darbar Square pillar has an image of Annapūrṇā at its top. Standing upon a lotus pedestal, the goddess is holding a brahmada ṇḍa in her right hand and a water vessel in her left hand. She is wearing a crown and a long garland. Inscriptions have been written on the south and west faces of the pillar. One of these inscriptions records the destruction caused by the earthquake and the progress of the recovery work. In addition to this, it also details some of the development works undertaken by Juddha Śamśera. The inscription states that many people were helped by Juddha Śamśera, who donated 1 million 74 thousand and 913 rupees. It also records the amount of money collected in the assistance fund and its expenditure.

label: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya
description: The Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya is located at Kotā Ṭola to the north of Dey Pukhu. Its vedikā stands on a rectangular platform. Above the vedikā one can see a lion throne that displays sculpted images of four lion figures and Caturmahārājas on the four corners and at each of the cardinal directions, respectively. The Four Buddhas have been placed on a throne located on the upward opening single-layer lotus blossoms. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi are located on the eastern, southern, western and northern faces of the caitya respectively. Akṣobhya’s seat is decorated with images of two elephants and Maitreya. Similarly, the south side shows two horses and Vajrapāṇi, the west side displays peacocks and Padmapāṇi, and the north side contains images of Garuḍas and Mañjuśrī. Three layers of lotus petals can be found above the Buddha statues and small statues of the Four Buddhas and Four Tārās are placed above these petals. Cement plaster has been used to join the caitya's garbha and harmikā . The yaḥsĩ has also been plastered with cement. The structure of the caitya suggests that it can be dated back to the 19-20th century. According to the local residents, it was built by a Tulādhara family. Remnants of a collapsed phalcā lie to the north of the caitya . Local residents assume that a stone inscription is buried somewhere in this rubble.

label: Baku Nani
description: Baku Nani is one of the courtyards within the Itum Bāhāḥ Ṭola. It is located to the south of Itum Bāhāḥ ( KAT1220 ). Local community members believe that it is named after the fact that the Nani is located at the lower part of the extended Itum Bāhāḥ courtyard. There is a shrine in the middle of the Nani. A caitya is consecrated inside it, which is the only heritage property in the Nani. Similar caitya examples are also present elsewhere in front of the Itum Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, in Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, and in Kāyegu Nani. There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of this caitya . In an inscription inside the sanctum from 1853 CE (NS 973), it is mentioned that the caitya was renovated. In the inscription, the caitya is referred to as Vajradhātu Caitya. Both Pruscha (1975, 44) and Locke (1985, 290) mention that the temple was constructed in a traditional way and tiled with jhĩgaṭī bricks. However, the temple's entire structure transformed into a cemented construction when it was renovated in 1987 CE. A Śākya family residing in the nani takes care of the temple and performs daily worship. Previously, on certain days every month, devotees gathered around the temple to recite mantras and other religious texts. This tradition takes place in the present-day twice a year on the full moon day of Kārttika and during the Kathmandu Pañcadāna Festival. On the full moon day of Kārttika, the local residents display various images made of fried pulses and grains. This tradition also continues to this day.

label: Ṭīkā Bhairava at Bhelachẽ (c. mid-16th cent. CE)
description: Measuring 367 x 367 cm in size, the west-facing Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is located in the Bhelāchẽ Tol, to the north of the Durbar Square of Patan. Ṭīkā Bhairava is also known as Unmatta Bhairava or Mahā Bhairava. The Bhelāchẽ Tol was named after this temple; its name derives from the Nevārī word bhelā, meaning Bhairava, and 'hẽ, meaning house. The main entry gate to the temple is to the west and is flanked by two guardian lions, which in turn have two metal flags between them. In front of the main entry, one can find a brick-paved space that contains several small objects. One of these is a stone Padmapatra, sitting almost at the centre and in line with the main entrance. One can also find a stone trough of an abandoned jarḥũhiti , which measures 50 cm in width and 173 cm in length. The lower banner on its right-hand side is broken. The Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is a three-storey pagoda-style temple, and stands on a low stone base. All three roofs of the temple are made of copper sheets. Above the entrance is a garuḍa toraṇa showing an image of Bhairava with eight hands. Bhairava is holding gajacarma, ḍamaru, katṛ and kapāla with his right hands, and gajacarma, khaṭvāṅga and naramuṇḍa with his left. The last hand is in a bindu position. Bhairava is at the centre of the toraṇa and is flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra. Behind the toraṇa is a window with a wall painting of Khyā on its left and an image of Kavã on its right. Below the second roof, in front of the window on the western side, one can find a wooden toraṇa with images of similar deities painted in different colors. At the top of the temple is a pinnacle with serpents in its four corners. A banner hangs down from the pinnacle to the bottom of the temple's first roof on the western side. The sanctum is a colonnaded space with 12 octagonal columns standing in three bays on each side. The central area within this space is demarcated by a 2.1m long wall of 70 cm thickness and two timber posts. Together, these form a square space; the main image of the deity, which faces to the west, is attached to the wall. However, the sanctum does not contain a stone image of the main deity. Instead, there is a metal śivaliṅga , with an image of Bhairava painted on the wall behind it. To the left of the śivaliṅga is a stone image of Gaṇeśa with four arms, and to its right hand side is a stone image of Kumāra, also with four arms. Uutside, the temple has twenty struts supporing the lowest roof. The four corner struts contain images of śārdūla , while the other 16 struts display images of the Eight Mātṛkās and Eight Bhairavas. Alongside this, the struts to the west also contain images of Rudra Bhairava mounted on a human being, Māheśvarī, Unmatta Bhairava mounted on a lion, and Brahmāyaṇī. The southern struts display Bhairava mounted on a human being, Mahālakṣmī, a Bhairava riding on a horse, and Cāmuṇḍā. To the east, the struts contain images of Bhairava mounted on a bull, Indrāyaṇī, Kapāla Bhairava riding on a snake, and Vārāhī. Finally, the northern struts display images of Bhairava mounted on a Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī, Pracaṇḍa Bhairava mounted on a boar, and Kumārī ( Tachikawa 2004,17-19). In the temple area are a bell, a jarũhiṭī , a small stone image of Basāhā and an aniconic stone image of Ajimā. According to Pruscha (1975, 176) this temple was built in 1541 but no inscription could be found to provide evidence of this date. Mention of this temple is, however, made in Kīrtipatākā , a text composed by Kunu Śarmā. It describes images of gods drawn on the walls of the temple (see in Naraharinātha 1961, 12).

label: Dune Bāhāḥ (1659 CE)
description: Dune Bāhāḥ, one of the branches of Oku Bāhāḥ ( LAL2260 ), is located in Okubāhāl Ṭola to the north of Oku Bāhāḥ. This Bāhāḥ can be accessed from two directions: either from the western side through a narrow alley between the houses opposite Mahābuddha Temple ( LAL2340 ), or from the south through another alley passing through an open courtyard. The monument building can be found on the west side of the courtyard and faces east. The principal façade has a main central door that is decorated with carvings of floral details and images of the Buddhist deities. The door is flanked by two narrow openings on either side. The ground floor of the building has been plastered in cement and painted white. It is separated from the first floor by a band of carved timber cornices. A pāsukājhyaḥ with three openings can be found at the centre of the first floor with two small arched windows on either sides. Above the central window, one can find a blind window with five arched recesses; these symbolise Pañcabuddhas. This floor was recently reconstructed using local deśī apā on mud mortar (writing in 2019). The structure is covered with a sloped CGI sheet roof, and is surrounded by tall, five-storey buildings on three sides. The courtyard contains a central Buddha shrine with three tiers (3.7m high), a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (50 cm high) and a Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya (1.7 m high). This Bāhāḥ was established by Punaju Śākya of Oku Bāhāḥ in NS 779 (1659 CE), which is why it is also called Pūrṇacandra Vihāra. Earlier, the god house of the monastic building had three storeys, however it was severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. As a result, the third floor has since been removed, and a roof of corrugated zinc sheets has been installed on top of the second floor. The façade of the first floor has a trikhājhyāla with a carved toraṇa; this is flanked by two small windows. Above the window, five niches made from terracotta symbolise the Five Buddhas. The ground floor houses the sanctum, which contains an icon of an east-facing Akṣobhya sitting in a bhūsparśa gesture. Dharmacakra Mañjuśrī sits to the left of the figure, whilst a statue of Avalokiteśvara can be found to its right. The entrance to the sanctum is flanked by two small windows but has no toraṇa . Instead, images of Akṣobhya Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara can be found above the door. A statue of a four-handed Ganeśa is housed in a niche to the right of the entrance (which lies to the south). Above this, there is a toraṇa with a further image of Gaṇeśa. Another niche to the left of the entrance (to the north) contains an image of Mahākāla; like the one on the right-hand side, this too is surmounted by a torana, this time displaying an image of Mahākāla.

label: Taleju Bell (13th cent. CE)
description: This large bell hangs on a stone structure between two stone pillars and has a metal roof with gajura s. It was built by King Jayavishnu Malla and Queen Chandra Lakshmidevi and used for special proclamations by the Malla Kings. It is now rung during Khadgajatra in honour of the Goddess Taleju ( Pruscha 1975, 162). The Taleju Bell is located between the Hariśaṅkara Temple and Cyāsiṃ Devala in the Patan Darbar Square. Similar large bells also constructed during the Malla period can be found at Basantapur Darbar Square (Kathmandu) and the Bhaktapur Darbar Square. This bell hangs on a stone beam supported by two stone pillars that are erected on top of a platform. To reach the platform, one must enter the inside of the plateau through a narrow door to the east of the building and climb up a ladder with 9 rungs. Above the beam, one can see a gilded copper roof, and on top of the roof there are three pinnacles topped with parasols. Small wind chimes hang down from the bottom of the roof, which in turn is supported by 16 struts. Statues of śārdūlas can be found on the struts positioned in the four corners, while other struts contain carvings of Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Bhairava and Mātṛkās. The body of the bell holds an inscription informing readers that it was commissioned by King Viṣṇu Malla (1729-1745) and Queen Candralakṣmī Devī. It also tells us that the work was supervised by general Mukunda Siṃha, and that this was paid for by the merchant Padma Siṃha. This inscription does not provide us any information about the intentions behind its construction. However, a Nepalese chronicle (see Bajracharya and Michaels 2016 , 129) states that the King installed this bell to scare his enemies. It is said that in the Malla period, this bell was rung to let people know that a royal announcement was about to be made; upon hearing the noise, people nearby would gather near the palace. It may also have been rung to tell citizens to come together for other special occasions. There is also a legend that the bell was rung daily in the morning and evening when the palace worshipped Goddess Taleju. At present, the bell may be sounded only during special occasions in the Dashain festival (for example when the demon-dancers come to dance in Mul Chowk and sacrifice animals). Only then is the small gate to the bell's platform opened.

Dathu Bāhāḥ (c. 1880s CE)
description: Dathu Bāhāḥ is a member of the branch of Mayūravarṇa Mahāvihāra and is situated southwest of this monument. It is one of three bāhāḥs that are located near to the Mayūravarṇa Mahāvihāra at its southeast corner. Dathu is positioned in between these, which is how it gained its name. The Bāhāḥ can be accessed through an underpass underneath a residential building from the western Cidhaṃ Bāhāḥ ( LAL2070 ). This Bāhāḥ has been built on the eastern wing and faces west. At present, however, it consists only of a ground floor, and this is also in ruins. Before 2015, this site was a three-storey Bāhāḥ complex. Three plain windows were installed on its first floor, and a secret room was located on this level. The second floor contained a trikhājhyāḥ flanked by two plain windows. The roof of the Bāhāḥwas made from zinc sheets. However, the first and second floors collapsed during the 2015 earthquake. Although the ground floor was badly damaged, the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ has remained safe. The ground floor has three colonnaded bays on its main facade; the central bay holds the main door. The space between the columns on the right-hand side is filled with brick masonry, while a small entry way can be found on the left. The architecture shows that this Bāhāḥ has stood witness to different periods of time. The main door is well carved and once was surmounted by a ṭoraṇa thã held up by stone lions, however the ṭoraṇa was removed after the earthquake. Historical photos show that the first and second floor contained a single opening window and a triple-bay window ( svapājhyaḥ ) respectively. The back wall (to the east) has been heavily damaged and parts of it have collapsed. The main sanctum room has been covered with CGI sheets to protect it from rain. The courtyard (8.95m x 7.25m) is paved in telia tiles, and contains a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala and a Śikharakūṭa Caitya (160cm high) lined up in the central axis in front of the main sanctum (to the west). The courtyard is still filled with debris from the collapsed building materials. Inside the sanctum, the stone statue of the seated main deity, Akṣobhya Buddha, faces west. The original statue was stolen some time between 1983-1985. Later, a similar statue was enshrined and covered with a metal garment. After the 2015 earthquakes, however, the metal garment of the deity disappeared. A small stone Caitya and a stone with sculpted images of four donors has also been preserved inside the sanctum. Before the earthquake, there was also a wooden tora ṇa dated NS 1004 with an image of Akṣobhya in the middle, Prajñāpāramitā on the right and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara on the left ( Locke 1985 , 87). After the earthquake, broken pieces of the tora ṇa were found scattered around, but the piece containing the date could not be located. The pinnacle which was once fixed on top of the toraṇa can now be seen above the entrance. Images of Hanumān and Mahākāla also survived the earthquake; they are now placed to the north and the south of the entrance.

Yatkhā Bāhāḥ Caitya
description: There are only few examples of big caityas constructed in the center of a bāhāḥ courtyard. Its shape closely resembles a Vajradhātu Caitya found in abundance in the Valley. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are located in niches facing east, west, south, and north respectively. The caitya ’s harmika , toraṇa , trayodaśabhuvana , and its pinnacle are covered with copper gilt. A ya ṣṭ hī is installed inside it. It is one of the oldest caityas in the Valley with its old ya ṣṭ hī remaining intact ( Gutschow 1997, 24). Locals believe that there is an Aśoka Caitya inside the caitya ’s garbha ( H. Śākya NS 1099, 31). There is scant inscriptive evidence to appoint caitya ’s initial construction. H. Śākya writes that the caitya ’s current look dates back to the nineteenth century. In 1868 CE (NS 989), an individual named Cikidhana Tāmrākāra renovated the caitya, and offered a gilt cakrāvalī and parasol at the top of the caitya . During this renovation, the caitya ’s ya ṣṭ hī was also replaced. A statue of Lokeśvara carved from the original ya ṣṭ hī is kept safe inside the caitya ’s garbha ( H. Śākya NS 1099, 46-46) . It was also renovated in 1976 CE (VS 2035). In the present-day (in 2021 CE), the Federal Government is renovating residential buildings, the dyaḥchẽ , and caitya ’s plinth. A local Udāy Guṭhī organises the anniversary of the caitya on the full moon day of Asauja (Āśvina). Tutaḥ Guṭhī members recite strotras in front of the caitya during the entire month of Guṃlā as well as on other auspicious days.

label: Dabū Phalcā (1704 CE)
description: This free-standing three-bay Phalcā faces east and is located in the north of Thati courtyard. Dabū Phalcā contains carved wooden pillars ( dhaliṃkhvāḥ) and small windows which can be dated back to the 17th century. Six old columns with kalasa motifs, a capital showing a dragon, small windows and rare panels have been preserved. The Phalcā's roof is covered with jhĩgaṭī tiles and has been recently repaired by a Khaḍgī at his own cost. Inside, one can find two inscriptions and a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara. The chariot of Matsyendranātha stops at the Thati Ṭola for several days, where it rests in the public space between this and two other phalcās . One of the inscriptions in this Phalcā mentions that it was constructed in 1704 CE (NS 824) by Narahari Bhāro and his wife Vasumuni, residents of Dhopogatra (present Dhaugala ṭola) during the reign of Yoganarendra Malla. The same inscription mentions the construction of a stage platform ( dabū ), though this has since been removed. The second inscription states that Siddhivajra Vajrācārya from Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra recited Guṇakāraṇyavyūha at the chariot procession of Matsyendranātha in 1868 CE (NS 988). The inscription does not mention whether the recitation took place inside the Phalcā or somewhere else. The building was reconstructed one month after this recitation took place. A representative of each of the four major Vihāras of Patan was involved in both the recitation and the reconstruction process. No religious or cultural activities are observed here any longer.

Amṛta Hiti
description: Amṛta Hiti, locally known as Pvaḥ Hiti, was constructed during the medieval period for the Poḍhe community residing in Imūkhel, Lalitpur. The hiti has two water conduits, facing east. Generally, statues of Bhagīratha are installed under the water spout(s) of a hiti , however, this is not the case in Amṛta Hiti. A statue of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu is established on the hiti ’s northern wall which S. Khanal (2068, 173) dates to the sixteenth and seventeenth century. The source of water for this hiti originates from the hillock of Imūdvã. Due to rapid urbanization, the underground water level is depleting, hence the hiti dries up during winter and flows only during the monsoon season. There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of the hiti . However, it is probable that it was built sometime during the medieval period ( Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 45). It was renovated by the local community in 1988 CE (VS 2045). The UN-Habitat and Integrated Urban Development Project assisted to form a local committee in 2008 CE (VS 2065) for the management of water collection from the hiti during the night and distributing it to the public during the day. However, this plan did not work out. The local community cleans the hiti on the day of the Sithinakhaḥ, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.

Nārāyaṇa Mandira (ca. 1803 CE)
description: The Nārāyaṇa Mandira (Temple) is located inside the Bāghabhairava Temple Complex ( KIR0004 ) in Kirtipur. The door to its sanctum which is ornately designed and carved, rests on a stone pillar base ( īlvaha ṃ ) and is flanked by a pair of stone lions. Generally, such a type of door architecture can be seen only in tiered temples. Thus, we can assume that the Nārāyaṇa Mandira too was originally a tiered-styled temple. There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this Temple. However, Ś. Śre ṣṭ ha (VS 2057, 45), without refereeing to any sources, mentions that it was constructed by Hastikā (one of the nannies of King Raṇabahādura Śāha) in 1803 CE during the renovation of the Bāghabhairava Temple ( KIR0004 ). The Temple’s pinnacle is octagonal and is gilded. According to the elders of this area, the octagonal gilded pinnacle was established by a certain Jītavīra (who was supposedly a government employee), a resident of the Tuṃjhvaḥ Ṭola (Kirtipur) when he renovated the Temple in 1932 CE (VS 1988) by the order of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera (r. 1 September 1932 - 29 November 1945). The inscription inscribed on the pinnacle records this information. It was probably during this renovation the temple’s structure was changed from a tiered style to a domed style. Such a domed style temple architecture was popular during the time of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā. From his time onwards, several damaged temples were reconstructed in the domed shape. The present look of the Nārāyaṇa Mandira dates back to 1952 CE (VS 2009). Around the same time, a gu ṭ hī was established to look after the Temple and conduct the daily rituals here ( Ś. Ś ṛ e ṣṭ ha , 1994, 87). A statue of Śrīdharaviṣṇu standing on the samapāda posture is consecrated inside its sanctum. The statue has four arms: he is carrying a cakra (wheel) on his upper right hand and a gadā (mace) on his upper left hand. Similarly, a padma (lotus) is on his lower right hand and a śan ̇ kha (conch shell) is on his lower left hand. The Śrīdharavisṇu statue is flanked by a Sarasvatī (left) and Lakṣmī (right) statue. These two female deities are believed to be Viṣṇu’s wives in the Kathmandu Valley from the medieval time ( R. Vanta VS 2061, 19). Beside these, a statue of a donor couple in greeting posture ( namaskāramudrā ) is also erected inside the sanctum. The descendants of Jītavīra who had renovated the Temple in 1932 CE used to clean the Temple premises, paint the Temple and perform its anniversary rituals. They had also endowed some plots of land for this purpose. However, this tradition came to an end sometime during the decade of 2000s CE (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).

Cibhāḥkhyaḥ Caitya
description: Cibhāḥkhyaḥ Caitya is located at Kaṅkeśvarī, Kathmandu. It is constructed on a relatively open space and this city quarter is named Cibhāḥkhyaḥ after the caitya . It has a three-level plinth, constructed with bricks, and plastered with bajra mortar. There is a staircase on the western façade of the caitya . Statues of four Buddhas are placed in its four cardinal directions. Dissimilar to many other caityas , the shape of Chibhāḥkhyaḥ Caitya’s dome ( garbha ) is unique (see the monument photos). Motifs of four Buddhas are kept on the hali ṃ pau above the harmikā. The local community members believe that this is one of the Aśoka Caityas and was constructed by King Aśoka himself. It is believed that the place, where the caitya stands, was a pond of milk ( durupukhū ), Aśoka filled it, and constructed the caitya . However, there is no evidence to verify these beliefs. Pruscha (1975, vol. II, p. 38) mentions that a person called Kelayel Tuladhar constructed this caitya . However, neither there is evdience to prove this claim, nor the local elders are aware of it. Pruscha might have misspelled the above-mentioned name. Some of the local elders believe that the Śreṣṭhā family who runs the Hotel Ambassador at the Lazimpat Road, Kathmandu, constructed Chibhākhyaḥ Caitya. The caitya was renovated in 1983 CE (VS 2040) after a tree, sprouting out of the caitya ’s upper part, t rayodaśabhuvana , threatened to topple it. In the present-day, no one worships this caitya . Previously, the above-mentioned Śreṣṭhā family members used to worship it on the full moon day of Vaiśākha. A local community member, named Radhākṛṣṇa Śāhī, takes care of the caitya in the present-day.

Śākyamuni Buddha Shrine (consecrated in 1957 CE)
description: The Buddha statue enshrined in this small shrine is one of the biggest statues in Balambu. The shrine is located west of the street leading to the southern gateway to the city. The statue (which faces) east is constructed out of a single stone. The Buddha exhibiting the bhūmisparśamudrā is seated on a double-decked lotus throne placed on a stone plinth. Generally, Buddha statues are not adorned except for his classical features such as elongated ears, curly hairs, and half-closed eyelids. This motif is followed here too. An inscription below the statue states it was established by Śakhalāla, his wife Āsāmāyā and their two daughters in NS 1077 (1957 CE). Around a decade ago, iron railings were welded around the statue for its safekeeping. Around the same time, a roof was constructed above the statue and was capped by a metal caitya (local knowledge, Maharjana, male, 63 years). Pruscha (1975, 155) has published a photo of this statue before the railing was installed. Śakhalāla’s family members take care of the statue. However, they do not perform any anniversary rituals. The members of the local communities worship the statue here on auspicious occasions, such as procession, festivals and so forth.

Bhindyaḥ Hiti
description: Bhindyaḥ Hiti is located next to the Bhīmasena Mandira in Bhīmasenasthāna Ṭola, Kathmandu. Dissimilar to many other hitis in the Kathmandu Valley, Bhindyaḥ Hiti has only one water spout, facing east. A makara motif is carved on the conduit of the hiti and a statue of Vidhyādhara and Umāmaheśvara are respectively installed below and above the conduit. Add to this, statues of Bhagīratha, Gaṇeśa, Candra, Lakṣmī, and alike, as well as a śivali ṅga are also established in the hiti premises. The Kathmandu Municipality has placed a huge plastic water tank to the northwest of the hiti . The municipality fills it with tankers to distribute water to local residents when the hiti runs dry during the non-monsoon seasons. There are no evidences to date the initial construction of the hiti . The iconographic program of the statues found in the hiti premises suggest that it could have been built sometime during the Late Malla Period (1482-1768 CE). The stone inscription (from NS 942, i.e. 1822) installed in the hiti premises records the a pavement of the road above the hiti and of the yard in front of the Bhīmasena Mandira. Bhindyaḥ is one of the few hitis still in use. It is a major source of water for the local community during the monsoon. Unfortunately, it merely drips during the non-monsoon seasons. Local residents believe that washing clothes and taking shower in the hiti in the past contributed to its sullied appearance. Thus, a local club, Youth for Nation Nepal, has prohibited to wash clothes and take shower in the present-day. Water from this hiti is compulsorily used for the daily rituals in the nearby Bhīmsena Mandira. Once in every twelve years, the Bhīmsena statue is shifted to a secret room inside the temple. At the end of this ritual, this statue is ritually cleaned with the water collected from the hiti . The above-mentioned club and the local community periodically clean the hiti premises.

Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha
description: Four aniconic stone statues representing various deities are established inside the Pīṭha. They are adorned with toraṇa , one of which is larger than the others. The local community worships it as the Indrāyaṇī. There is another kīrtimukhatoraṇa behind this statue and a large tree growing behind the Pīṭha. A phalcā and a hiti is constructed nearby the temple. Indrāyaṇī’s statue, brought from the deity’s god-house (dyaḥchẽ ), is exhibited here during auspicious occasions. Thrice every year, the deity’s chariot procession is organised and is taken around the city quarters of the core city. The local community, especially from the western part of Bhaktapur, come here to worship on their birthdays and conduct kalaḥpūjā . Devotees throng to the temple on the eighth, ninth, and tenth day of Dasaĩ festival. Some of them also offer animal sacrifice during Dasaĩ.

label: Siddhimukteśvara Mandira (1855 CE)
description: Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī constructed the temple at the Pacalī Ghāṭa in the memory of his father Siddhinārāyaṇa Rājabhaṇḍārī in 1854 CE. Siddhimāna also constructed Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa ( KAT2636 ) and Dhaneśvara Mandira ( KAT2638 ). The temple was consecrated on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in 1855 CE (VS 1911). A stone śivali ṅ ga, which was brought from India, is consecrated as the main deity inside its sanctum. Siddhimāna was one of the trusted elites of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā and fiercely supported the Rāṇā regime. He was a subbā in 1846 CE, and in 1859 CE, he became a treasurer ( khajāñcī ). He was appointed as the governor for Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, and Kanchanpur districts, collectively known as the Nayā Muluka ‘New Kingdom’ in 1864 CE. Siddhimāna played a significant role in the economic upliftment of these districts ( Adhikari 1984, 219). He also accompanied Jaṅga Bahādura to his official state visit to the Great Britain in 1850 CE ( Rana 1974, 116). He had also established a gu ṭ hī and endowed land to sustain the daily worship in this temple. However, neither the endowed land nor the gu ṭhī exist in the present-day. Previously, a Brahmin priest was appointed as the priest to perform the daily rituals and he was paid a monthly salary of four thousand rupees. In the present-day, Viṣṇudevī Rājabhaṇḍārī, Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī’s fifth-generation daughter-in-law, performs the daily worship in the temple. She also operates a home for elderly in the temple premises. The anniversary celebration of the temple takes place every year on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha. On the day of Śivarātri, a big light ( mahādīpa ) is lit in the temple premises and a special worship is performed on the birthday of Kṛṣṇa (Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī). A person called Rāmacandra Thāpā, who runs a paint shop in Ṭeku, Kathmandu, has been painting and repairing the temple from time to time.

Gopāleśvara Mandira
description: The temple known as Gopāleśvara houses a śivaliṅga and is situated on the cremation site of a sage named Gopāla Muni. The temple features a dome-shaped structure and faces south, located on the path between Sūryaghāṭa and Kailāśa. It has a central finial on top of the dome, and although there were originally smaller finials on the four corners of the roof, only two remain (as of June 2023). The temple's substructure is made of brick and contains the sanctum where a four-faced ( caturmukhī ) śivaliṅga is enshrined as the main deity. East of the temple is the Sūryaghāṭa Śivālaya ( PPK1612 ) ensemble. Inside the sanctum, there is a statue of Hanumān on the western wall, and a square-shaped hollow space designated for fire oblations. The temple has entrances on all four sides with brick arches ( toraṇa ). The exact date of the temple's construction is unclear, but its architectural style suggests that it was built during the Rāṇā period. The śivaliṅga inside the sanctum was installed around 2022 CE by devotees. The temple premises were neglected and unclean for many decades until devotees took the initiative to clean and develop it into a place suitable for meditation. Unfortunately, the temple was already in a dilapidated state when it was further damaged by the earthquakes in 2015. No priest is formally appointed for the temple. Instead, a person from the Nepālī caste has been taking care of the temple for the past 25 years. Due to its serene location, the temple area has become a popular spot for meditation, and the number of people visiting for this purpose has increased over the years. On the auspicious occasion of Śivarātrī, which falls on the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, a bonfire is set up in front of the temple. Other socio-religious activities are not regularly conducted at this temple.

Thokreya stone memorial pillars
description: The pillars are located on both sides of the track, 15 minutes to the south-west of the village of Thokreya. Thokreya is found at a few kilometres south-west of Dullu. The four pillars are oriented to the south and display a variety of decorations. Pillar 001 is not decorated. Pillar 002 contains two circular motifs on the top, that probably represent the sun and the moon, or stars. Below it are traces of inscription. Pillar 003 is partly buried and tilted, but it remains possible to see a central stūpa, surmounted by three circular motifs. Pillar 004 is broken in vertically broken in half. The top of the stele is occupied by a large flower motif with eight petals. Below is an eroded inscription where one can read 'śake 1330' (1408 CE). All of the pillars show traces of metal tools sharpening. Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century. They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors. In this case it is possible to situate the Thokreya stone memorial pillars between the 14th and the 15th century on the basis of their shape and the inscription of 1408 CE on pillar 004 (see Andolfatto 2019 : p. 108).
